Manufacturers charged to deploy AI, energy-efficient technologies to cut costs
items.description: By Yinka Kolawole The Manufacturers Association of Nigeria (MAN) has urged manufacturers to embrace Artificial Intelligence (AI), advanced technologies and energy-efficient solutions to tackle rising production costs, strengthen energy security and improve industrial competitiveness. The call was made at the 2026 Manufacturers Energy Security and Energy Efficiency Summit in Lagos, where industry leaders and government representatives examined the role of technology, sustainable energy supply and structured financing in addressing the energy challenges confronting Nigerian manufacturers. The event was jointly organised by Manufacturers Power Development Company Ltd. (MPDCL), GIZ and the Nigerian Energy Support Programme (NESP). President of MAN, Ifeanyi Okoye, said the industrial energy cost reduction and adoption programme would promote factory rooftop solar installations, battery energy storage systems, captive natural gas solutions, and smart energy management networks. He said the programme was aimed at addressing the rising cost of energy, which had significantly affected manufacturing operations and competitiveness. According to him, manufacturers spend about 40 per cent of their profits addressing energy challenges, while high electricity tariffs, unreliable grid supply, and dependence on fossil fuels continued to undermine industrial production. “The summit is to facilitate access to long-term financing instruments, climate funds, green investments, and asset-financing mechanisms to support manufacturers’ transition to more efficient energy systems,” he said. In his comment, Director-General of MAN, Segun Ajayi-Kadir, said the adoption of emerging technologies had become critical to improving production efficiency, reducing energy consumption and strengthening the resilience of manufacturing operations. He noted that AI and smart manufacturing systems could help industries optimise energy use, minimise production losses, lower operating costs and improve product quality, particularly amid persistent electricity supply challenges. Chairman, Board of Directors, MPDCL, John Aluya, noted that the high cost of self-generation had reduced manufacturers’ profit margins and weakened their competitiveness. He stressed that reliable and affordable energy was critical to the survival of Nigerian industries, adding that the summit was meant to explore practical solutions, including solar photovoltaic systems, battery energy storage, captive gas power, energy efficiency, and carbon credit monetisation. In his keynote address, Ulf Brackmann, Chief Executive Officer of IKAPITAL Family Office & Friends, said AI could significantly boost industrial productivity and create new employment opportunities rather than displace workers, urging manufacturers to take advantage of the opportunities offered by technological innovation. Brackmann however noted that AI could only cut costs and boost efficiency for manufacturers where factories have dependable electricity and sound digital foundations. He warned manufacturers against seeing AI as an instant solution to their production challenges. “AI is very often seen as a magic pill or sold as a magic pill to manufacturers as if it would solve all the problems. No, it doesn’t,” he stated. The post Manufacturers charged to deploy AI, energy-efficient technologies to cut costs appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Power outages, rising costs slow manufacturing growth —NESG
items.description: By Yinka Kolawole Frequent power outages, rising production costs and limited access to credit are slowing manufacturing growth in Nigeria, with businesses struggling to sustain operations amid persistent infrastructure challenges, the October 2026 Business Confidence Monitor (BCM) by the Nigerian Economic Summit Group (NESG) has shown. The report indicated that manufacturing remained in expansion territory in October, but its Current Business Performance Index declined to 107.3 points from 108.4 points in September and 111.3 points in October 2025, reflecting a moderation in business activity. It identified incessant power outages, inadequate raw material supplies, high rental costs, limited access to credit and infrastructure deficiencies as major constraints confronting manufacturers during the month. According to NESG, these challenges continued to amplify operating costs, despite sustained expansion in business activities across the economy. The impact was particularly evident in key manufacturing subsectors. Textile, Apparel and Footwear slipped into contraction territory, with its performance index plunging to 99.7 points in October from 127.5 points in September. Cement also remained in contraction at 94.5 points, while Food, Beverage and Tobacco was the only one of the three major manufacturing subsectors to record improved performance and remain in expansion territory. The report’s findings underscore the growing burden of unreliable electricity on manufacturers, who depend on stable power supply to sustain production lines, process raw materials and maintain factory operations. Frequent outages force businesses to rely on alternative energy sources, adding to production costs and weakening their competitiveness. At the broader economy level, Nigeria’s Current Business Performance Index moderated to 115.4 points in October from 117.8 points in September, although it remained above the 111.3 points recorded in October 2025. All sectors remained in expansion territory, but only Trade and Services recorded improved performance compared with the preceding month. Agriculture, Manufacturing and Non-Manufacturing experienced slower growth. The cost pressures were also reflected in the NESG’s business indicators. The cost of doing business sub-index stood at 45.2 points in October, while the prices sub-index was 65.5 points, both significantly below the 100-point neutral threshold, indicating that most firms continued to face elevated operating costs and producer prices. Despite the challenges, the Future Business Expectations Index rose to 130.8 points in October from 128.9 points in September, signalling improved optimism about business conditions over the next one to three months. Manufacturing recorded an expectations index of 145.1 points, behind Trade at 194 points, but ahead of Non-Manufacturing at 135 points. NESG attributed the improved outlook largely to expectations of stronger consumer demand during the year-end festivities and ongoing campaign activities. The post Power outages, rising costs slow manufacturing growth —NESG appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Pourquoi Hakim, ingénieur brillant, a-t-il quitté une banque de renom pour ouvrir une sandwicherie ?
items.description: Hakim est un ingénieur au parcours remarquable, spécialiste des mathématiques appliquées et de la statistique. Diplômé d’une grande école française, il rejoint rapidement une institution bancaire de renom, où il s’épanouit pleinement en tant qu’ingénieur d’études en statistiques mathématiques. Ce poste lui apporte à la fois satisfaction intellectuelle, stabilité professionnelle et reconnaissance sociale. Un jour, au détour d’une rue, il croise un ami d’enfance, désormais propriétaire d’une modeste sandwicherie. Au fil de la discussion, cet ami lui lance une remarque aussi simple que troublante : « Travailler dans une banque est haram (illicite), car cela repose sur la riba (usure), interdit en islam ». Quelques mots, une affirmation catégorique, et une conviction qui s'installe. Quelques mois plus tard, Hakim démissionne. Il laisse pousser sa barbe, adopte le qamis et entreprend de réorganiser son existence autour d'une pratique religieuse qu'il souhaite désormais plus exigeante. Il finira par ouvrir, lui aussi, une sandwicherie. Cette histoire, qui peut sembler anecdotique, soulève pourtant des questions importantes sur les transformations religieuses et sociales de notre époque. Des parcours de rupture plus fréquents dans nos sociétés Un tel revirement de vie n’est pas courant, mais il n’est pas isolé non plus. En y regardant de plus près, ce phénomène n’est pas propre au monde musulman. On observe des trajectoires similaires ailleurs : des traders devenus moines, des ingénieurs devenus prêtres, des médecins engagés dans des causes spirituelles ou écologistes, des cadres reconvertis dans des modes de vie ascétiques… Il s’agit souvent de parcours de rupture, nés d’un sentiment d’inadéquation entre ce que l’on fait et ce que l’on juge juste. Cela étant, la situation est un peu différente pour Hakim. Eh bien qu’elle puisse surprendre, je peux comprendre – et dans une certaine mesure respecter – sa démarche, ainsi que celle d’autres jeunes dans son cas, surtout lorsqu’elle n’est pas motivée par un rejet de la raison ou par un caprice, mais par une volonté sincère d’aligner ses actes sur ses convictions religieuses. Cependant, au-delà de la question purement théologique – l’islam interdit-il réellement de travailler dans une banque conventionnelle ? – se posent des interrogations bien plus vastes et profondes : Pourquoi une affirmation aussi catégorique semble-t-elle avoir suffi à emporter sa conviction, sans qu'il éprouve le besoin d'examiner les différents arguments et les avis juridiques existants ? Et comment se fait-il qu’il choisisse systématiquement l’avis le plus strict, alors même qu'il existe, parmi les savants et les instances de jurisprudence musulmane, des avis divergents sur certaines activités exercées dans les banques conventionnelles, notamment selon la nature des fonctions et les responsabilités assumées ? Un sentiment d’impuissance face à cette dynamique La réponse à ces questions ne réside pas uniquement dans le savoir ou le statut social. Elle tient aussi à une quête de sens, à ce besoin universel de cohérence morale et spirituelle qui transcende les diplômes et les carrières. Parfois, il suffit d’une phrase, d’un mot, pour raviver une vérité enfouie. Et ce déclic ne vient pas toujours d’un théologien ou d’un intellectuel, mais d’un visage familier, d’un ami sincère ou d’un homme simple mais convaincu. Ce phénomène révèle aussi une tendance marquante de notre époque : on observe chez certains jeunes, y compris parmi les plus diplômés, un malaise moral vis-à-vis de certains secteurs professionnels, perçus comme incompatibles avec leurs valeurs, ainsi qu'une forme de déconnexion plus générale à l'égard de l'éthique spirituelle. Ce qui me trouble le plus, c’est le sentiment d’impuissance que j’éprouve face à cette dynamique. Car si la démarche de Hakim peut se comprendre sur le plan spirituel, certaines de ses conséquences, notamment lorsqu'elle conduit à ériger une interprétation particulière en norme générale pour les autres, méritent d'être sérieusement interrogées. Après sa démission, il a traversé une période de transition professionnelle, durant laquelle il a notamment bénéficié du RSA, avant d'ouvrir à son tour une sandwicherie. Il passe aujourd’hui une grande partie de son temps à la mosquée, où il s’efforce de convaincre d’autres jeunes de suivre son exemple. Face à cela, on se sent souvent démuni. On a beau mobiliser le Coran et la Sunna, évoquer les finalités du droit musulman (maqâsid), rappeler les priorités ou s’appuyer sur le raisonnement par les conséquences (fiqh al-ma'alat), ces arguments ne semblent pas toujours parvenir à infléchir des convictions désormais profondément ancrées. Il s’agit là d’un basculement intime, qui échappe à toute logique argumentaire, mais qui exprime quelque chose de profond sur notre époque : le besoin de sens, et le désenchantement de certains jeunes face au monde tel qu’il est. Il faut continuer à tenter de convaincre. Mais plus encore, il faut espérer que le temps fera son œuvre — ce qui, malheureusement, n’est jamais garanti. Un appel à la responsabilité des théologiens, des intellectuels et des imams Il est temps que nos institutions religieuses, nos conseils théologiques, nos intellectuels et surtout nos imams prennent pleinement la mesure de cet enjeu. J'en appelle particulièrement aux imams, qui sont quotidiennement au contact de notre jeunesse. Ils ne peuvent rester en retrait face à ces évolutions. Ils ont une responsabilité essentielle : accompagner les jeunes dans leurs questionnements, leur apporter des éclairages théologiques solides et leur apprendre à distinguer les principes fondamentaux de la religion de leurs différentes interprétations. Nous avons besoin d'une parole religieuse qui ne se contente pas d'énoncer des interdits, mais qui explique, contextualise, hiérarchise et éclaire. Une parole capable de conjuguer la fidélité aux textes, la connaissance des réalités contemporaines et la compréhension des finalités de la religion. Il ne s'agit évidemment pas de défendre une religion de facilité ni de relativiser les prescriptions islamiques. Il s'agit de rappeler que la piété ne se mesure pas à la sévérité des positions adoptées, que la prudence ne doit pas devenir une source d'interdictions systématiques et que la divergence juridique, lorsqu'elle repose sur des arguments sérieux, constitue une richesse de notre tradition. Nos théologiens et nos intellectuels doivent également investir davantage cet espace de réflexion et de transmission. Nous ne pouvons pas laisser les discours les plus catégoriques occuper seuls le terrain, tandis que les approches savantes, nuancées et contextualisées peinent parfois à atteindre les jeunes. Notre responsabilité n'est pas de convaincre les jeunes de choisir une banque plutôt qu'une sandwicherie. Elle est de leur donner les moyens de réfléchir, de discerner et de faire leurs choix en connaissance de cause. Car une foi véritablement éclairée ne demande pas de renoncer à son intelligence : elle invite au contraire à la mettre au service de la connaissance, de la sagesse et du bien commun. *Azzedine Gaci est recteur de la mosquée Villeurbanne (France) Important : Les tribunes publiées sur TSA ont pour but de permettre aux lecteurs de participer au débat. Elles ne reflètent pas la position de la rédaction de notre média. items.title: ACAMB advises bank customers against phishing scams
items.description: The Association of Corporate Communication and Marketing Professionals in Banks (ACAMB) has urged bank customers to remain vigilant against phishing scams and other forms of cyber fraud, warning that criminals are increasingly using fake bank alerts, cloned websites and impersonation accounts to steal sensitive financial information. The warning follows a fraudulent text message impersonating various banks. FactCheckAfrica debunked the message, finding that the link it contained led to a cloned internet banking website designed to steal customers’ login credentials, BVNs, card details and transaction PINs. The incident highlights the risks associated with digital banking fraud in Nigeria. In June, Wema Bank suspended its engagements on X, (formerly known as Twitter) amid reports of more than 70 fake accounts impersonating the bank and its ALAT platform. In August, Zenith Bank Plc disclosed that it was investigating unauthorised access to customer data linked to a global cyberattack. ACAMB President, Jide Sipe, warned that fraudsters were increasingly adopting sophisticated methods to impersonate trusted banking brands and steal customers’ personal information, making their schemes difficult to distinguish from legitimate communications. “When a scam message carries your name, your phone number or your bank’s logo, it looks real. That is exactly why customers must slow down. No bank in Nigeria will ask you to confirm your PIN, password, OTP or BVN through a link,” Sipe said. Sipe acknowledged the efforts of banks to strengthen fraud detection and customer protection, alongside regulatory measures introduced by the Central Bank of Nigeria’s mandatory cybersecurity self assessment guide. He stressed, however, that these efforts must be complemented by customer awareness and vigilance, particularly when handling requests for sensitive banking information. “Banks can strengthen their security systems, but fraudsters continue to find ways to exploit unsuspecting customers. We must all remain vigilant. Always pause, verify requests through official channels and report anything suspicious before taking action,” he added. Sipe urged customers to avoid clicking links in unsolicited messages asking them to verify, reactivate or secure their bank accounts. He also warned against sharing personal identification numbers (PINs), passwords, one-time passwords (OTPs), card verification values (CVVs) or BVNs in response to suspicious requests. Customers should verify such requests directly with their banks through official mobile applications, verified social media accounts or published customer service numbers. items.title: World Ports Confab: FG woos global investors with maritime reforms
items.description: By Godwin Oritse The Nigerian Ports Authority (NPA) has intensified efforts to attract global investment into Nigeria’s maritime sector by showcasing the Federal Government’s ongoing port reforms and investor-friendly policies at the World Ports Conference, highlighting opportunities for private sector participation, improved port efficiency and sustainable growth. Speaking at the ongoing World Ports Conference in London, Managing Director of the Nigerian Ports Authority, Dr Abubakar Dantsoho, showcased President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s maritime policies and its positioning of Nigeria’s Ports as Africa’s biggest economy that is yearning for global investment. He affirmed that the speed of growth and development in the country’s ports signifies the huge opportunities investors should tap into, adding that the current administration of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu has put policies in place that are investment friendly. The NPA boss identified Nigeria’s huge population, urbanization, and infrastructural gaps in the ports as attractive opportunities for investment in its maritime and associated sectors. Dantsoho, who is also the Vice- President of the International Association of Ports & Harbours (IAPH) and doubles as Chairman of the Port Management Association of West and Central Africa (PMAWCA) told investors that Africa’s untapped resources remain the best destination for ports investment and development. He said the government alone cannot fund development of bigger or deeper sea ports and other similar projects hence the need for investors to take advantage of such opportunities across the continent. Dantsoho affirmed that “Nigeria has the highest population in Africa. So, the speed of growth is something that really should concern us. For example, in Nigeria, only recently, about 3 years ago, we commissioned the first deep sea port in Nigeria, which is called Lekki Deep Sea Port, that was funded by the Chinese government in relationship with China Harbor, and the expenditure cost us $1.6 billion to build Lekki in Lagos. items.title: BoI advocates investment in industrial clusters to boost Lagos economy
items.description: By Babajide Komolafe The Bank of Industry (BOI) has called for increased investment in industrial clusters, reliable power supply and supporting infrastructure to boost productivity, attract private capital and strengthen the Lagos State economy. Managing Director/Chief Executive Officer, BoI, Dr. Olasupo Olusi made this call in a keynote address delivered at the 4th edition of the Lagos Economic Outlook 2027 Discourse, themed, ‘“Development Pathways, Emerging Risks and Strategic Policy Priorities.’ Represented by Dr. Isa Omagu, General Manager, MD/CEO’s Office, BoI, Olusi said investment in industrial clusters, particularly along major industrial and port corridors, would help businesses overcome production constraints, reduce operating costs and improve their competitiveness. He also said Lagos must assess economic progress by the improvements businesses and residents experience, rather than relying solely on economic growth figures and public spending. “The test is whether Lagos becomes more productive and more liveable,” he said. He identified electricity costs, traffic congestion, access to appropriate financing and institutional coordination as major constraints to business productivity. “A manufacturer needs reliable electricity. A worker needs a commute that does not consume productive hours. Firms need predictable approvals, appropriate finance and customers,” he said. Olusi urged the state to prioritise investment in power infrastructure serving industrial clusters, faster freight movement, streamlined business approvals, flood-resilient commercial routes and skills development. Speaking at the event, Lagos State Commissioner for Economic Planning and Budget, Mr. Ope George, said the ministry would continue to coordinate economic intelligence, development planning, budget management and performance monitoring in support of Lagos State’s long-term development aspirations. He said the 2027 economic outlook provided an opportunity to consolidate the state’s achievements, address structural challenges and strengthen its position as a competitive and resilient economy. “Our focus goes beyond economic projections. It is about shaping policies that will strengthen competitiveness, promote inclusive growth and secure a sustainable future for Lagos State,” George said. Earlier, Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Economic Planning and Budget, Mrs. Olayinka Ojo, highlighted the state’s development planning, budget monitoring and performance evaluation frameworks. She said Lagos was strengthening evidence-based governance through its long-term development plan, Medium-Term Expenditure Framework, annual budgets and regular monitoring of revenue, expenditure and project delivery. Ojo also highlighted the government’s engagement with communities and the use of platforms to improve citizens’ access to information on public projects and social intervention programmes. items.title: Customs frees 98 containers of power equipment stranded for 20 years
items.description: •Cargoes to ease pressure on substations, strengthen national grid — Tegbe By Udeme Akpan The Nigeria Customs Service (NCS) has released 98 containers of electricity transmission equipment stranded at the nation’s ports, some for up to 20 years, in a move expected to strengthen the national grid and improve electricity supply across the country. The Minister of Power, Joseph Tegbe, disclosed this in Lagos, stating that 44 containers were released from ENL Terminal, while another 54 were cleared from APMT and Sun & Moon Terminals. He said the 98 containers represented part of more than 300 containers of transmission equipment held at the ports. The equipment, comprising high-capacity transformers, cables and switchgear, was procured to expand the transmission network, address overloaded substations and improve electricity delivery nationwide. Tegbe said: “The equipment was procured to expand the transmission network and relieve overloaded substations. Its detention stalled projects, kept existing substations under heavy strain, exposed valuable assets to deterioration and accumulated charges on the cargoes.” He noted that the prolonged detention of the equipment had imposed additional costs on businesses, households and public institutions, which continued to grapple with unreliable electricity supply. Also speaking, the Comptroller-General of Customs, Bashir Adeniyi, said the Service had commenced processes to clear the containers in collaboration with the Ministry of Power, the Nigerian Ports Authority and terminal operators. He said: “The release follows the President’s directive for immediate clearance and for agencies to resolve outstanding charges and administrative bottlenecks without delay.” Adeniyi pledged to work with the Minister until all the containers were cleared, while appealing to terminal operators to support the national effort. The Minister disclosed that an inspection of the recovered equipment showed that most of the items remained useful and viable. He said: “When evacuated, it will be verified, tested and refurbished where necessary, then deployed to project sites to complete stalled installations, relieve overloaded substations and strengthen constrained transmission corridors.” The post Customs frees 98 containers of power equipment stranded for 20 years appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Sam George engages global telecom leaders at MWC Doha 2026
items.description: Ghana’s Minister for Communication, Digital Technology and Innovations, Samuel Nartey George, has joined international policymakers and telecommunications industry leaders in Qatar for the 2026 edition of the Mobile World Congress (MWC), with discussions focused on expanding digital cooperation and strengthening global connectivity. The three-day event officially opened on Sunday, November 8, at the Doha Exhibition and Convention Centre. It is being organised by the Global System for Mobile Communications Association (GSMA) in partnership with Qatar’s Ministry of Communications and Information Technology. The congress has brought together governments, international organisations and private-sector players to deliberate on emerging technologies, telecommunications development, digital innovation and opportunities within the global digital economy. As part of Ghana’s participation, Mr George took part in the Digital Leadership Forum, which examined key developments in the telecommunications industry, as well as the GSMA Ministerial Programme. The latter provides a platform for ministers, heads of delegation and industry leaders to discuss the future of connectivity. He is also expected to attend the State of Qatar Ministerial Roundtable, where ministers and senior officials will explore how digital transformation can support a more inclusive, sustainable and resilient future. The Minister’s engagements include bilateral discussions with counterparts from the Bahamas and Kenya on areas of mutual interest, voting and candidacies, as well as aligning policy positions. The meetings are intended to strengthen Ghana’s international partnerships and advance its interests in telecommunications and digital governance. Mr George is further scheduled to attend an informal meeting of heads of delegation ahead of the formal proceedings and the Commonwealth Evening Reception hosted by the Commonwealth Telecommunications Organisation (CTO). Ghana’s participation in MWC Doha 2026 forms part of its broader engagement with international partners on digital development, innovation and policies aimed at widening access to connectivity and creating opportunities for citizens and businesses.

items.title: Huayou, seeking control of Ghana’s Ewoyaa lithium mine, faces scrutiny over compensation delays in Congo
items.description: Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt, the Chinese company seeking to acquire Atlantic Lithium, the developer of Ghana’s Ewoyaa lithium mine, is facing scrutiny in the Democratic Republic of Congo over delayed compensation to communities affected by pollution from one of its subsidiaries. Congo’s mines ministry said on November 6, 2026 that Congo Dongfang International Mining (CDM) remains obliged to pay $6 million to affected communities, despite financial difficulties and a suspension of its operations, Reuters reported . The development comes as Huayou advances its investment in Ghana’s proposed first lithium mine. Atlantic Lithium shareholders are scheduled to vote on the proposed takeover on December 14, following court approval. The Congo case concerns an industrial wastewater spill at CDM’s Lubumbashi operation in November 2025. According to the Congolese ministry, a basin intended to retain water had been used to store acidic solutions. The incident affected surrounding communities and prompted authorities to suspend the company’s operations for three months. Authorities subsequently required CDM to provide $2 million each to Kasapa, Kamatete and Kamisepe. A separate $6.6 million penalty was imposed for payment to the state treasury. However, implementation of the community compensation programme has been delayed. The ministry attributed the delays partly to financial difficulties cited by CDM, which recently announced that it had halted its activities. “Financial difficulties or the suspension of operations do not exempt the operator from its obligations toward affected populations,” the ministry said. For Ghana, the development draws attention to the environmental and community obligations of the group moving into Ewoyaa. Huayou’s involvement in the project is already progressing independently of its proposed acquisition of Atlantic Lithium. The company has completed an agreement to acquire Elevra Lithium’s rights and interests in the Ewoyaa project and Ghana portfolio. The proposed acquisition of Atlantic Lithium remains a separate transaction, subject to shareholder approval, regulatory approvals from Ghana’s Securities and Exchange Commission and the Ministry of Lands and Natural Resources, alignment with the Minerals Income Investment Fund, and the fulfilment of the remaining conditions. Minister for Lands and Natural Resources, Emmanuel Armah-Kofi Buah The Congo incident does not establish that similar problems will arise at Ewoyaa. It does, however, provide a record against which Ghanaian regulators and affected communities can examine the proposed investor’s environmental safeguards and arrangements for compensation. The issue extends beyond whether a company can finance a mine. It is also about whether its obligations to affected communities can be enforced when financial difficulties force it to suspend operations.

items.title: 2026 Lagos Trade Fair: We’re poised to turn stability into prosperity — Tinubu
items.description: By Yinka Kolawole President Bola Tinubu has said Nigeria’s next economic priority is to translate the gains of ongoing reforms into prosperity through enterprise, industrial growth and expanded trade. Tinubu spoke at the weekend, at the opening of the 40th Lagos International Trade Fair, organised by the Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry (LCCI), at Tafawa Balewa Square, Lagos. The president, represented by the Minister of State for Industry, Senator John Enoh, said the Federal Government had made significant progress in stabilising the economy, adding that the focus must now shift to stimulating production, creating jobs and expanding business opportunities. “The emergency is over. The foundation has been repaired. Our task now is to turn stability into prosperity, and enterprise is at the heart of that task,” he said. Highlighting the administration’s economic achievements, Tinubu said Nigeria’s gross external reserves rose to approximately $55.07 billion in October 2026, the highest level in 18 years, while net reserves exceeded $40 billion, from less than $4 billion in 2023. He also noted that inflation declined to 14.63 per cent in September 2026, while the economy grew by 4.43 per cent in the second quarter, describing the figures as evidence of improving economic fundamentals. On trade, the President said non-oil exports exceeded $6.1 billion in 2025, while capital importation reached about $21 billion, expressing optimism that Nigerian businesses could leverage the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) to access wider markets. He, however, stressed that sustainable economic growth must be driven by domestic production and value addition rather than dependence on imports. Tinubu said the National Industrial Policy provides a roadmap for strengthening manufacturing, deepening local value chains and converting Nigeria’s raw materials into finished products. He disclosed that the Ministry of Industry, Trade and Investment and its agencies supported more than 115,000 micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) in 2025, promising continued efforts to improve their access to finance, electricity and markets. He described industrial and trade policies as complementary, stressing that while industry provides goods for export, trade creates markets for locally manufactured products. The President also welcomed exhibitors from more than 20 countries and said Nigeria would host the Intra-African Trade Fair for the first time in 2027, in partnership with Afreximbank. items.title: Analysis: Presidency says new national airline is viable. Government should publish the reports
items.description: The Presidency says preliminary studies have confirmed that Ghana’s proposed national airline is viable. “Preliminary studies have affirmed the viability of the project”, the presidency said in a social media post on November 6, 2026. However, the announcement does not disclose further details or the assumptions behind that conclusion. The statement followed President Mahama’s meeting with Boeing officials, who are supporting efforts to establish the airline. Source: Presidency According to the Presidency, an agreed roadmap includes identifying strategic and technical partners, obtaining an Air Operator Certificate, selecting aircraft and deciding how the business will be financed. These decisions will help determine how much it costs to establish and operate the airline. With several still outstanding, the preliminary studies would help explain the conditions under which the project is considered viable. The announcement did not include those studies. The government began the process to establish the national airline in May 2025, when Transport Minister Joseph Bukari Nikpe inaugurated a 10-member task force. Its mandate was to develop a sustainable business model for the proposed national carrier. A Ministry of Transport document indicates that a business model and operational framework report has been developed to guide engagement with a strategic investor. Source: Transport Ministry, PBB However, the full report is not publicly available. It is also unclear whether it contains the preliminary studies cited by the Presidency or represents a separate assessment. That distinction matters. A proposed ownership structure explains how an airline might be organised. A viability assessment should explain whether it can attract enough passengers and revenue to cover its costs, and what happens if it cannot. The government has already outlined one important feature of the proposed arrangement. Mr Nikpe has indicated the government intends to remain a minority shareholder, with the private sector leading operations and management. That could help strengthen commercial discipline. But the size of the government’s shareholding alone will not determine how much public money is at risk. The financing arrangements matter too. A government can hold a minority stake while guaranteeing loans, supporting aircraft leases, or agreeing to cover specific costs. The report should therefore explain the government’s expected contribution, any obligations beyond its initial investment, and whether further public support would be limited. If the airline runs into financial difficulty, who would provide the additional money? That question matters, given Ghana’s previous experience. Ghana Airways ceased operations in July 2004 after five consecutive years of losses. An IMF assessment published the following year identified weak financial oversight, costly aircraft decisions, borrowing, and free or discounted tickets for government workers as factors behind its debt buildup. Source: IMF, August 2005 A new ownership arrangement would need to show how it intends to prevent these problems from recurring. A change in shareholders will mean little if the underlying weaknesses in financial oversight and management remain. This includes how the board and chief executive would be appointed, who would approve borrowing and procurement, and whether management would be free to make commercial decisions about staffing, fares and routes. Private sector leadership could provide that protection. Whether it does will depend on the agreements governing the airline and how they are enforced. The same scrutiny should apply to the proposed strategic partner. The government must explain how the partnership would be structured, including how responsibilities, risks and returns would be shared. A foreign partner’s participation is not, by itself, a guarantee of commercial success. An established airline could bring investment, technical expertise and access to a wider network. But the agreement would need to explain how those benefits would translate into a sustainable Ghanaian business, including training local staff and developing technical and managerial capacity. Beyond the ownership and financing arrangements, the studies should establish what gap the airline is intended to fill. The Presidency says the project would increase the use of Ghana’s airport facilities and support plans to make Accra a leading aviation hub in West Africa. It also projects thousands of jobs for pilots, cabin crew, engineers and aviation management specialists. Those ambitions require a clearer business case. Which routes would the airline serve? How much demand is expected? What would it offer that existing carriers do not? And how long would it take before the business could cover its operating costs? Benefits may extend beyond the airline’s finances, including tourism, cargo services, and improved connections to underserved markets. But those benefits should be assessed alongside the cost of securing them. The government should also explain whether other measures could achieve similar gains, including improving services at Accra International Airport, encouraging existing airlines to expand, or making Accra more competitive as a connecting hub through reduced fees, better infrastructure, and enhanced efficiency. Establishing a national airline may be part of the answer. The studies should show why. Publishing the reports would let the public assess these questions before making binding financial commitments. The government could withhold commercially sensitive details while releasing the main demand forecasts, cost estimates, financing assumptions, and safeguards for public funds. Ghana’s previous airline failures do not establish that another attempt will fail. They do, however, make it reasonable to ask what will be different this time. The government says preliminary studies support the project. It should release those studies and the task force’s report so Ghanaians can examine the business case before committing more public money and resources.

Mali: «À un moment, j’ai arrêté de compter les décès», témoigne El Bachir Thiam, ancien détenu de la Sécurité d’État
items.description: Au Mali, cela fait un peu plus d’un an qu’El Bachir Thiam est sorti des geôles de la Sécurité d’État du Mali. Membre du parti Yelema - aujourd’hui dissous, comme toutes les organisations politiques du pays -, il avait été enlevé le 8 mai 2025 à Kati, par des agents encagoulés des services de renseignements maliens, puis libéré après avoir passé près de cinq mois en détention en dehors de toute procédure légale. À cette période, plusieurs militants pro-démocratie avaient été enlevés dans les mêmes conditions, alors qu’un éphémère mouvement de contestation du régime en place émergeait, vite éteint, justement, par cette série d’enlèvements. Aujourd’hui en exil hors du Mali, il raconte les conditions de détention atroces, la mort de plusieurs dizaines de codétenus, les menaces de mort pour l’inciter à se taire... Il répond aux questions de David Baché.

items.title: The mounting debt burden should terrify Nigerians, by Dele Sobowale
items.description: •Tinubu seeks $20.5bn; €1.04bn foreign loans to fund projects – Vanguard, October 28, 2026 •Debt worse than leprosy, Obasanjo replies Tinubu — Report, October 31, 2026 Seldom do I find myself on the same side with former President Obasanjo on matters concerning national affairs. Right now, I am on all fours with Baba Iyabo with regard to his position on President Tinubu’s request for fresh loans amounting to over $21 billion or N29.4 trillion. The debt burden is now approximately N160 trillion. Given a shamelessly rubber stamp Senate, it is a foregone conclusion that it will be approved. By December, the total debt would total N189.4 trillion. It was about N100 trillion when Buhari left the nation’s “economy on the brink of bankruptcy” – according to Tinubu. Read Also: Economy: Food warehouses now split wholesale bags as retailers battle inflation Putting the request into historical perspective would help to understand the loan request better. From 1978, under General Obasanjo, when the first $2.8 billion loan was taken, it took the country 21 years until 1999 to accumulate $36 billion or N50.4 trillion at current exchange rates. Minister of Finance, Dr Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala got us out of the debt trap in 2004. By the time President Jonathan left office in 2015, the debt had risen to $30 billion or N42 trillion once again. Eight years of Buhari’s financial mismanagement racked up N58 trillion. By the time this fresh loan is approved and taken, Tinubu would have added N89.4 trillion in just three and a half years; and, this might not be the last loan request before May 29, 2027. Whoever is President next year might be facing a debt burden well over N200 trillion. When last year I wrote that borrowing is the opium of the governing classes, it never occurred to me that the addiction could be as bad as this. Obasanjo is absolutely correct; mindless borrowing, tainted with corrupt and concealed self-interest, is indeed worse than leprosy. Lepers sometimes have children without leprosy. The malady is invariably restricted to one person and one generation. Nigeria’s debt load, made infinitely worse by Tinubu’s fiscal policy mismanagement, is already visiting diseases more virulent than leprosy on millions of Nigerians alive; and will savage millions more for at least three generations for one inescapable reason – inability to repay from revenue generation. Revenue collection and ability to repay loans “Nigeria misses 10-month revenue target by N20.7tn” – Report, October 27, 2026. The report which must have been glossed over by most Nigerians, when taken in conjunction with a previous one which announced that debt repayment exceeded revenue collected, should raise alarm everywhere. Despite all the attempts to mislead Nigerians, the fact is; the Federal Government, FG, is living on borrowed funds. Nigeria is unable to pay its bills and repay loans, as and when due, without resorting to more loans. Like all addicts, this nation is hooked on loans and would suffer a major shock if borrowing stops. No nation develops rapidly by borrowing alone. That is a verdict of economic history which cannot be disputed. Another axiom of economics stipulates that governments must take the lead and determine the directions of growth and development; and not leave them to the haphazard and un-coordinated plans of the private sectors. Our current experience with the Dangote Refinery should serve as a lesson regarding what can happen when the government abdicates its role as the driver of the directions of growth to individual investors. Given unclear government guidelines with regard to production, pricing and distribution of fuel, Dangote is at liberty to export fuel – even when acute global scarcity induces high fuel prices locally. Consequently, the FG is forced to make promises which cannot be kept – reduced transport fares from October 1, more CNG vehicles, subsidized fuel for 30 days. Each failure reinforces distrust of government and makes it more difficult to stimulate support. Monetary policy management under the current Governor of the Central Bank of Nigeria, CBN, is the only aspect of the government which is encouraging foreign investors. The other areas of reform are not working so well – for the simple reason that fiscal policy management is falling short of expectations. Few people would have believed, until it happened, that Tinubu, a proclaimed accountant, would mismanage the annual budget worse than Buhari. Under Buhari, one year’s budget was extended by no more than six months. The 2025 Budget will run until December 2026; nobody is certain, if and when the 2024 Budget ended. Capital appropriations for 2024 and 2025 were less than five per cent of the amounts budgeted; and 2026 is already following the same pattern. Again, it has been demonstrated worldwide that rapid economic and social development is only possible with unrelenting infrastructural development. Three years’ performance unconvincing “LOANS: It’s not how much we borrow, but what we build – TINUBU” -Vanguard, October 30, 2026. Tinubu elaborated on that statement: “The real question is not how much we borrow, but what we build, what value we create and what future we leave behind.” The statement is half true and half untrue. Obasanjo called it “nonsense”. I won’t go that far. Tinubu is absolutely correct when he asserted that “it is not how much we borrow but how much we build”. His references to the Lagos-Calabar, Sokoto-Badagry and Trans-Sahara highways exposed the weakness in his defence. Highways – Sokoto-Badagry for example – have been started before and abandoned later. The Sokoto-Badagry road, in particular, brings painful memories to my family. Started by Obasanjo in the mid-1970s, my immediate senior brother, Adebowale Sobowale, working for Texaco, was killed on the road, under construction on November 25, 1978. It was abandoned shortly after Shagari became President. The fact that construction starts does not guarantee completion. Governor Jakande started monorail in Lagos; Buhari cancelled it; Shagari embarked on the Third Mainland Bridge; Buhari stopped it; Babangida completed it. The truth is: with long-term and expensive projects, nothing is certain until they are completed. Even completion does not ensure economic feasibility or financial viability. Labour Transport, bank-rolled by the FG when Oshiomohle was President, never returned a kobo on investment. Over thirty airports and airstrips exist in Nigeria; only four are viable. The FG is now busy acquiring those disasters. Mere existence will not transform Kogi or Nasarawa airports to investment from absolute waste of public funds. Clearly, you can build; but “what we build” might constitute a heavier debt burden than a profitable investment creating jobs and increasing national wealth. We have seen it happen before. The Nigerian Airways was established with the intention of projecting the country abroad, creating jobs and making money as well. It ended in receivership, wiped out jobs and impoverished some of its creditors. All the governments involved in all those failed enterprises also once thought of “what future we leave behind”. Go to Ajaokuta and see what previous FGs left behind. My real fear “Habit is stronger than reason” – Professor William Dorfmann. My real fear is this; given a government addicted to debt, and given the addict’s habit of spending every kobo at hand, the new loan might not even be spent on the projects stated. What has Tinubu built with N60 trillion already borrowed? Vanguard News The post The mounting debt burden should terrify Nigerians, by Dele Sobowale appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Bangladesh's external debt increases almost threefold in decade
items.description: Bangladesh’s foreign debt has almost tripled in 10 years, a steeper rise than in any other South Asian country except the Maldives, according to the World Bank. Even so, the country has a lower debt burden relative to export earnings than Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Bhutan. However, its burden is higher than that of India and Nepal. According to the World Bank’s International Debt Report 2026, Bangladesh’s total foreign debt stood at $113 billion at the end of 2025, up from about $38 billion in 2015. That is the third-largest stock in South Asia.For every $100 in annual earnings, Bangladesh carries $210 in total debt and pays back $16 annually. Economists say the indicators are manageable for now, but Bangladesh could face repayment trouble if borrowing keeps growing at this pace and the money is not put to proper use. In the South Asia region, India holds the largest external debt stock at $764 billion, up 59pc in a decade. Pakistan follows at $135 billion, almost double the level of 10 years ago. In Sri Lanka, foreign loans rose 31pc to $57 billion. External debt rose 186.5pc to $11 billion in Nepal and 57pc to $3.3 billion in Bhutan. The Maldives recorded a more than fourfold increase to $4.7 billion. Repayments take 16pc of exports Debt servicing took 16pc of Bangladesh’s export earnings in 2025, 3.1 percentage points less than the year before. That is the share of export income spent on repaying principal and interest on foreign loans, and a falling ratio is a positive sign of repayment capacity. Even so, it remains above India and the South Asian average of 10pc, though below Sri Lanka at 26pc and Bhutan at 19pc. Measured against gross national income (GNI), servicing costs are low. At 2pc, Bangladesh matches India and the regional benchmark, against 5pc in Sri Lanka and 6pc in Bhutan. The country’s debt-to-GNI ratio, which is external debt as a percentage of the national income, stands at 24pc. It is a manageable level but slightly above the South Asian aggregate of 21pc. The ratio is 20pc in India, 41pc in Pakistan and 54pc in Sri Lanka. Set against what the country earns from exports, the debt looks heavier. External debt stands at 210pc of Bangladesh’s annual exports, more than twice what the country earns each year from foreign trade and other income. That is far above India at 83pc and the South Asian aggregate of 95pc, but below Pakistan at 324pc, Bhutan at 301pc and Sri Lanka at 272pc. Warning on borrowing Zahid Hussain, a former lead economist at the World Bank’s Dhaka office, said Bangladesh still does better than Pakistan and Sri Lanka on these indicators but trails India. “If foreign debt keeps growing at the current pace, it would not be surprising if Bangladesh eventually faced a situation similar to Sri Lanka’s,” said the economist. “If you are not prudent about the types of debt you take and how you use the borrowed funds, becoming another Sri Lanka is only a matter of time.” He said comparing Bangladesh with Pakistan is difficult, given Pakistan’s particular geopolitical and strategic situation. Zahid said exports matter because the debt-to-GDP ratio shows very little about a country’s ability to repay. A large economy is not enough; it also needs adequate liquidity, which is why the export ratio is important. On this measure, Bangladesh is also vulnerable because its export base is small and heavily dependent on a single product category. Its exports as a share of GDP are among the lowest, he said. “Remittances add to foreign currency earnings, but even counting them India stays far ahead because its remittance income is much higher. Sri Lanka, similarly, receives large numbers of tourists and earns substantial foreign currency from tourism,” he added. Costlier loans ahead Prof Mustafizur Rahman, a distinguished fellow at local think tank Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), said the debt-to-GDP and debt-to-export ratios are rising gradually, but the most important indicator is the ratio of net exports to debt servicing. He said that about 85pc of export earnings come from readymade garments, where domestic value addition is 60-65pc. The ratios would therefore be significantly higher if net exports were used. Recent loans carry relatively high interest rates and shorter repayment and grace periods, so the ratios will rise rapidly in the coming years, said Mustafizur, as Bangladesh already faces growing debt pressure. Government debt servicing was $4.9 billion in the last fiscal year and is projected to reach $7.6 billion by 2029, as interest rates climb while grace and repayment periods shrink. The interest rate in Japan, for example, has risen from below 1pc in 2021 to above 3pc, he said. He said Bangladesh needs to raise exports and domestic value addition, improve domestic resource mobilisation and reduce its reliance on foreign borrowing to finance the Annual Development Programme. “Global financing conditions are tightening. Bangladesh will still need foreign loans, but should negotiate better terms and secure more concessional financing,” he said, adding, “It could also consider raising funds through bond issuance.” According to the World Bank report, foreign debt of developing countries rose 5.5pc to a record $9.4 trillion in 2025, the fastest growth since 2021 and about four times the average pace of 2022-24. Debt-service pressure remained severe amid elevated global interest rates. Low and middle-income countries paid $1.4 trillion in principal and interest in 2025, up 1.9pc and the fifth consecutive annual rise. Between 2022 and 2025, developing countries paid $436 billion more in debt service than they received in new financing.—The Daily Star/ Published in Dawn, November 9th, 2026

items.title: 2027: I’ve no godfather but God — Makinde
items.description: By Luminous Jannamike ABUJA — The Presidential Candidate of Allied Peoples Movement, APM, Engr. Seyi Makinde, declared weekend he had no political godfather other than God, expressing confidence that divine backing and the support of Nigerians would propel him to victory in the 2027 presidential election. Read Also: ADC to APC: Test your popularity at polls, stop using courts to block us Makinde, who spoke at a church service organised by the Church of Christ in Nations, COCIN, Jos, Plateau State, yesterday, said Nigeria urgently needed a governance reset to address years of poor leadership, economic hardship and social challenges, particularly in the last three and a half years. He said the need to change the country’s direction informed his RESET NIGERIA manifesto he presented to the church leadership, describing it as a blueprint for making life easier for citizens. Makinde recalled how he defied the absence of political godfathers to become governor of Oyo State in 2019, expressing confidence that his presidential ambition would also be sustained by faith and popular support. “When I said in Oyo State in 2018 that I would like to be governor, somebody asked me, ‘Governor of which Rotary District?’ I said governor of Oyo State, and they asked, ‘with no godfather; nobody in politics who can stand in for you?’ I responded by saying, well, I have God the Father. And I became the governor of Oyo State. “This time around, we also have God the Father and that God will be merciful unto Nigeria and He will show us mercy in this country,” he said. The APM candidate said his administration in Oyo State was guided by planning, transparency and accountability, noting that he developed successive development roadmaps covering his first and second terms, from 2019 to 2027. He said the documents provided clear direction for his administration and helped ensured that promises made to the people were translated into concrete actions. Makinde said he had adopted a similar approach in preparing for the presidency, with the RESET NIGERIA agenda built around four pillars: security, the economy, education and the socio-political space. Presenting the manifesto, he challenged Nigerians to hold him accountable for the commitments contained in the document. “I want Nigerians to be able to hold me accountable, not just through promises but through documented commitments. Everything is written down in black and white, and I am prepared to be held accountable for everything contained in this document,” he said. He also urged Nigerians, particularly Christians, to participate actively in politics and prepare to exercise their democratic rights in the 2027 general election. “Please, get ready and participate. History is about to happen again,” he urged. Responding, COCIN President, Rev. Dr. Amos Musa Mohzo, drew Makinde’s attention to the country’s worsening insecurity and economic hardship, highlighting the challenges confronting Nigerians. While praying for the APM candidate, Mohzo encouraged him to continue his political journey, expressing confidence that God’s will would prevail in his destiny. Makinde is in Jos ahead of the APM presidential campaign rally scheduled for Monday at Rayfield Park. items.title: Iqbal and the Pakistani dream: fact or fiction?
items.description: Visiting Srinagar once, Indian essayist Pankaj Mishra found Iqbal in a rather unexpected place. Or, at least, in an unlikely heart. For most Indians, Mishra notes, Iqbal was simply the “misguided instigator of the movement for Pakistan.” But then Mishra met Mohammad Ishaq Khan, a historian of Islam in Kashmir. By his very nature, Dr. Khan held politics at arm’s length; his writing focused on faith’s quieter, more contemplative hues. And yet when this gentle scholar found himself at Iqbal’s tomb in Lahore, he was overcome. “I couldn’t control myself. Tears started pouring from my eyes.” Concluded Mishra, “The idea of Iqbal as the man who had brought a hope of redemption to the Muslims of the subcontinent survived, and—this is what struck me—still had the power, many decades later, of moving even someone like Dr. Khan, committed to the intellectual life, to tears.” That is, perhaps, the starting point: the debate over what Iqbal proposed in terms of Muslim statehood, reignited recently by social media, is secondary to how he made those Muslims actually feel—that after such protracted loss, there could yet be salvation. Or, as the poet himself put it, Sabaq phir parh sadaqat ka, adalat ka, shujaat ka / Liya jaye ga tujh se kaam dunya ki imamat ka . But while most already know Iqbal to be the answer to something inwards—to a crisis of the spirit—the material world stakes as much of a claim. Because, for the authors of the Pakistan project, it wasn’t quite enough that he set the youth’s hearts on fire; it was also necessary that the prestige of his name attach itself to the idea of Pakistan. An intellectual genesis requires, well, intellectuals, and few were more moving than the Allama. Nor did it hurt that the man was born, raised, and closely tied to the Punjab, a land both vital to, and late to join, the country’s creation. Geniuses were needed in Pakistan proper; otherwise it would be just too unbearably ironic that firebrands in UP, a place still stuck in India, would get to monopolise the origin story. Dreams of Pakistan: misreading Iqbal’s Allahabad address This is why Iqbal’s famous Muslim League presidential address, delivered in Allahabad in 1930, is a gift to Pakistan Studies. His core statement is as follows: “I would like to see Punjab, North-West Frontier Province, Sindh and Baluchistan amalgamated into a single state. Self-government within the British Empire, or without the British Empire, the formation of a consolidated North-West Indian Muslim state appears to me to be the final destiny of the Muslims, at least of North-West India.” For most nationalist histories, this is a watershed: the dream of Pakistan, put forward by the poet of the east for the first time—separate statehood from India (and, even more convenient, no awkward references to a Bengal that would require excising after 1971). But none of this is borne out by the record. For starters, separate statehood was not floated by Iqbal first: right-wing activist Murtaza Ahmad Khan Maikash wrote it up in a four-part-series in Lahore’s daily Inqilab in 1928, premised on the same four provinces that make up Pakistan today. A similar proposal by Malerkotla nawab Zulfiqar Ali Khan followed a year later. Second, a separate country wasn’t, in fact, floated by Iqbal at all—at least, not in 1930. He did wish for ‘Punjab, North-West Frontier Province, Sindh, and Balochistan’ to be ‘amalgamated into a single state,’ but, as he mentioned elsewhere in the same speech, the plan was to work “ within the body-politic of India.” When Iqbal said “state”, it was in the lowercase Indian fashion, as a province. Son Javid Iqbal confirms in his book Islam and Pakistan’s Identity that this was for a “Muslim India within India, as the word ‘state’ used by Iqbal, only implied the grant of full autonomy…” The poet clarified as much in his letter published in The Times on 12 October 1931: “I do not put forward a demand for a Moslem State outside the British Empire.” His view was that “Muslim provinces…would be the bulwark of India…against the hungry generations of the Asiatic highlands.” He wrote again of Hindu-Muslim ties in 1931, “…I cannot allow myself to believe…that all human efforts directed to uniting the two communities are doomed to failure.” For those still unconvinced, Iqbal put all doubts to rest in 1934, writing to friend Edward John Thompson his refusal to own “the scheme called Pakistan”: “You have made one mistake which I hasten to point as I consider it rather serious. You call me a protagonist of the scheme called Pakistan. Now Pakistan is not my scheme. The one that I suggested in my address is the creation of a Muslim Province i.e.; a province having an overwhelming population of Muslims in the North-West of India. This new province will be, according to my scheme, a part of the proposed Indian Federation. Pakistan scheme proposes a separate federation of Muslim Provinces directly related to England as a separate dominion. This scheme originated in Cambridge.” Iqbal signed off, “The authors of this scheme believe that we Muslim Round Tablers have sacrificed the Muslim nation on the altar of the Hindu or so-called Indian Nationalism.” Denying the Allama outright To those wary of state myths, a close reading of Iqbal’s address in 1930, and his own denials in 1931 and 1934, are enough to knock him off the pedestal of pro-Pakistan visionary. To be fair to the sceptics, the version taught in state textbooks is indeed wrong: Iqbal did not mean separate statehood in 1930; we know this because he literally said, over the next three years, that he meant nothing of the sort. His Allahabad address did not spell the dream of Pakistan; that we teach schoolchildren otherwise is a distortion of history. After all, as Iqbal himself implied, the seasoned politicians that found themselves at the Round Table had little in common with their critics. While Rahmat Ali and the angry young men of Cambridge were calling for a Pakistan that stood severed, the Round Tablers—Iqbal, Jinnah, and Zafrulla Khan—wanted Muslim security inside a federal India, secured by strong provinces and a weak centre. That’s why, at least up to 1934, Iqbal kept a safe distance from ‘the scheme of Pakistan’. Future foreign minister Zafrulla Khan went further and scoffed that it was “chimerical and impracticable”; that it was “a student’s scheme” with “nothing in it”. Jinnah was more generous, telling Rahmat and his friends, “My dear boys, don’t be in a hurry; let the waters flow and they will find their own level.” To say Iqbal thereby doesn’t figure in Pakistan’s genesis, however, is unkind. Firstly, because the waters did find their level: the Iqbal-sceptics play up his early denials without ever mentioning how his thoughts evolved on the subject: his final stance is best measured by his letter to Jinnah in 1937, which we will come to in a moment. Second, the Iqbal-sceptics also skip over the context: Muslim nationalist thought had not breached the frontier of separate statehood in 1930; not to any serious reception anyway. Jinnah himself was a decade out from calling for another country. When that did happen in Lahore in 1940, it was because two years of humiliation under Congress rule had offered a preview to formerly pro-union Muslims of what lay in store. They responded accordingly. Journey to separation: Iqbal’s 1937 letter to Jinnah By the time of the Lahore Resolution, however, Iqbal was gone. Pakistan’s national poet died in 1938—all of two years before the Muslim League’s major bid for separation, and before a hostile press helped dub that bid ‘Pakistan’. But not before the Allama’s remarkable mind had grasped the nature of the change; it’s why his politics would travel quite some distance from his initial Round Table position of the early 1930s. Hence, also, the irony: where he ultimately landed was far closer to the same Cambridge kids he had once distinguished himself from not too long ago. That Iqbal’s ideas underwent a slow-burn radicalisation in the last years of his life—as opposed to a sudden Damascus moment—is plain. “It is obvious,” he wrote of the rising Nehru, “that the Indian nationalist whose political idealism has practically killed his sense for fact, is intolerant of the birth of a desire for self-determination in the heart of North-West Indian Islam.” The resulting nationalism, wrote Iqbal, “can mean nothing but mutual bitterness and even oppression.” This lends a certain tenor to his crucial letter of 21 June 1937. “We are actually living in a state of civil war which, but for the police and military, would become universal in no time,” he warned Jinnah. But if a “storm” was coming to northwest India, Iqbal wrote, Jinnah was the only Muslim “to whom the community has a right to look up for safe guidance.” And, in a big departure from his Allahabad address, Iqbal now declared that the “idea of a single Indian federation is completely hopeless.” What, then, was the cure? As he wrote to Jinnah, “A separate federation of Muslim provinces…is the only course by which we can secure a peaceful India and save Muslims from the domination of non-Muslims. Why should not the Muslims…be considered a nation entitled to self-determination…?” Over seven years, Iqbal the federalist had become Iqbal the separatist. Three years later, Muhammad Ali Jinnah stood before an exultant crowd in Lahore and joined him. A reason to fight Like the lawyer he placed his dying hopes in, Iqbal is too often painted in absolute shades. Yet as we have seen, he was neither the first-ever-dreamer of Pakistan in 1930, nor was he its rejectionist by the close of his life in 1938. But then, at the risk of repetition, the whole debate is secondary. Because, compared to the common sense of the Quaid, Iqbal stirred something visceral in the young Muslim. No dense political theory, including Iqbal’s own, could replicate the primal forces his poetry unleashed: a gasp for dignity that could only ever find its most cogent expression in the birth of Pakistan. Perhaps it was the waters finding their level again. Nor did they ebb, even after 1947. “What Iqbal means to me”—and it can only ever be the ‘me’—Nietzschean, confessional, boundless—is a subculture of its own in this country. Iqbal didn’t dream up Pakistan so much as he provided a basis for the Pakistani dream: a voyage of self-discovery; a reason to fight. Without him, Muslim nationalism would have remained a pair of broken wings. And most everyone knew it. Jinnah said he would take Iqbal’s works over “the rulership of the Muslim state”. Ayatollah Khamenei called his young theocracy “the embodiment of Iqbal’s dream”, and anguished that the Iran before it was unfit for the poet to set foot in. Imran Khan, driven to despair by his mother’s death, sought out Iqbal as “a philosophy of action”—”that human beings were the makers of their own destiny.” All told, Iqbal was sui generis : the same sentiment that caused liberal intellectuals like Mohammad Ishaq Khan to weep at his tomb drove doctrinaire radicals like Khadim Hussain Rizvi to rage through police barricades. Bear in mind, also, that most of the above were inheriting a world that had spun far beyond Iqbal’s. But the poet was, like everyone else, of his time, and the spiritual upheaval he caused can best be gauged by the record of those years. For one contemporary in 1935, the 24-year-old Malik Ghulam Nabi, Iqbal’s masterpiece, Bal-e-Jibreel ( Gabriel’s Wing ), landed like thunder from the sky; a cry for freedom like none before. “It beat back our holy men…it knocked down the pseudo-socialists, it mocked the colonizers, it inspired the poor to stand on their own feet…those once ashamed of calling themselves Mussalmans now claimed it with heart-bursting pride.” Ghulam Nabi knew, because he was one of them. “As a student, I called myself G. N. Malik…Hindu friends made this out to be Gopal Narain or, in the Sikh tarang , Guru Nanak…it was Iqbal’s aihsaan that we were able to do away with this inferiority complex, and openly announce we were Muslims.” (Malik Ghulam Nabi would go on to join the freedom movement; his daughter-in-law, Dr. Yasmin Rashid, remains in prison.) That is, at its simplest, what Iqbal meant to so many. “The fate of the world has been principally decided by minorities,” he said once. “…Character is the invisible force which determines the destinies of nations, and an intense character is not possible in a majority.” And as the anxieties of a minority became those of a civilisation, it could only fall to Iqbal—a man of extraordinary contradictions—to become its poet-saint.

items.title: ADC to APC: Test your popularity at polls, stop using courts to block us
items.description: By Luminous Jannamike ABUJA—African Democratic Congress, ADC, has dared the ruling All Progressives Congress, APC, to test its popularity at the ballot box, rather than resort to court processes to frustrate the opposition party’s participation in the 2027 general election. Read Also: What is 25% requirement in Nigeria’s presidential election? The challenge came from the Director-General of ADC Presidential Campaign Council, Senator Austin Akobundu, who said the massive reception accorded the party’s presidential candidate, Atiku Abubakar, in Sokoto State, and his running mate, Rotimi Amaechi, in Kebbi State, reflected growing public enthusiasm for the party and the desire for an alternative political direction. In a statement yesterday, Akobundu, while thanking supporters and residents who turned out to welcome the candidates, accused the federal government and APC-led administration of attempting to shut the ADC out of the political contest through what he described as a backdoor judicial process. “If the federal government and the APC believe they have the capacity to win, let them allow a free and fair election. Let Nigerians choose without intimidation, obstruction or interference. “They must stop trying to muzzle the political space, using a backdoor court process to remove us from the contest,’’ he said. On the need to protect democratic competition, Akobundu insisted that Nigerians must be free to listen to competing political ideas, attend rallies and choose their leaders without interference. “The ballot must remain the people’s choice, and every party must be allowed to campaign freely,” he said. While urging party supporters not to be distracted by the political tensions, the ADC campaign chief called for restraint and sustained grassroots mobilisation. “Let us continue to campaign peacefully and confidently, knowing that the people’s will must prevail,” he pleaded. Akobundu said ADC would continue to take its message of affordable living, opportunity and national renewal to Nigerians across the country, while expressing appreciation to those who welcomed its candidates in Sokoto and Kebbi states. items.title: ADB launches Green-Grow scheme to empower smallholder vegetable farmers
items.description: Agricultural Development Bank (ADB) PLC has launched its Green-Grow Vegetable Farmers Lending Scheme to expand access to structured agricultural financing and boost local vegetable production. The initiative reinforces ADB’s commitment to agricultural transformation, financial inclusion, and sustainable agribusiness development, while positioning the Bank as a strategic financing partner in efforts to strengthen Ghana’s domestic food production capacity. The first phase selected and disbursed allocated funds to eligible smallholder vegetable farmers operating under irrigation in the Greater Accra and Volta Regions, with plans to expand to other areas. The scheme aims to address one of the major challenges facing smallholder farmers: limited access to affordable, timely financing to acquire essential farm inputs, improve productivity, and maximise returns. ADB’s Commitment to Agricultural Transformation Commenting on the initiative, ADB PLC Managing Director Edward Ato Sarpong emphasised the Bank’s commitment to supporting productive sectors of the economy, particularly agriculture. “Ghana’s agricultural transformation must be driven by deliberate investments that empower farmers to produce more, earn more, and contribute meaningfully to national development. Through the Green-Grow initiative, ADB is expanding its agricultural financing mandate. We believe that when farmers succeed, communities prosper, businesses grow, and the national economy becomes stronger,” Edward Ato Sarpong said. The ADB MD noted that the initiative reflects the Bank’s determination to move beyond traditional banking by developing innovative, commercially sustainable financing solutions that directly address the needs of agricultural producers. He further underscored the importance of strengthening domestic food production and building a more resilient agricultural sector capable of responding to changing market demands. Driving Financial Inclusion and Sustainable Growth The Deputy Managing Director of ADB PLC in charge of Services (DMD Services), Prof. Ferdinand Makafui Ahiakpor, described the scheme as a strategic intervention to bridge the financing gap in Ghana’s agricultural value chain. “Access to appropriate financing remains a critical factor in unlocking the full potential of Ghana’s agricultural sector. Green-Grow represents a practical approach to making agricultural credit more accessible, structured and responsive to the realities of smallholder vegetable farmers. “Our objective is to support viable agricultural enterprises, improve productivity and create sustainable economic opportunities across farming communities,” the DMD Services said. Prof. Ahiakpor explained that the scheme’s structured lending approach would help align financing with farmers’ production activities while promoting sound credit management and long-term financial sustainability. He said strengthening agricultural financing requires a balanced approach that supports farmers’ growth while maintaining responsible lending standards. Supporting Farmers, Strengthening Local Production The General Manager for Agribusiness at ADB PLC, Mr Kwame Asiedu Attrams, explained that the initiative followed preliminary field engagements with vegetable farmers across selected communities in the Greater Accra, Eastern and Volta Regions. The engagements identified promising financing opportunities among irrigated vegetable producers, particularly farmers with established production experience, market linkages and strong repayment potential. “Our engagements with farmers revealed enormous production potential that is being constrained by inadequate access to financing and the high cost of credit. Green-Grow has been carefully designed to address these challenges by providing structured credit support to eligible farmers,” Mr Attrams said. “By connecting financing to viable production activities, we aim to help farmers improve yields, expand their operations and take advantage of emerging market opportunities,” he added. Mr Attrams said the pilot would initially focus on vegetable production, taking into account seasonal conditions and market demand. The scheme’s eligibility criteria will be guided by factors including access to irrigation, farming experience, group cohesion, and a satisfactory credit history. Growing Ghana’s Agricultural Future The Green-Grow Vegetable Farmers Lending Scheme marks another step in ADB’s efforts to strengthen agricultural value chains and support the development of commercially viable farming enterprises. The initiative is expected to increase local production, strengthen farmers’ economic opportunities, and contribute to Ghana’s broader agricultural development objectives. The Bank is investing not only in farms, but also in the people, businesses, and communities that will shape Ghana’s agricultural future.
