items.title: Flight from reality
items.description: PAKISTAN’S ruling elites devote inordinate time and attention to foreign engagements — at the expense of tackling domestic challenges. The country’s media also tends to focus more on foreign policy and international events than on fundamental problems confronting the country. Switch on any TV channel and most talk shows are endlessly discussing Pakistan’s overseas forays, defence agreements, and other global developments. Some of this is understandable as a war in the neighbourhood and regional and international dynamics do have implications for Pakistan that merit comment. But domestic issues more consequential to the country’s fate and future rarely receive the same attention. There may be several reasons for this. For ruling elites, foreign engagements are a way to access and collect geopolitical rents to keep the economy afloat, enabling them to avoid undertaking domestic reform. Their notion of ‘success’ rests on foreign alignments that can deliver these rents without having to expend political energy solving structural economic problems at home. Hence, the almost obsessive focus on foreign pursuits and lack of reform at home. For governments resting on dubious electoral mandates, it is also the means to acquire international legitimacy to compensate for its absence at home. This is more so for authoritarian and hybrid regimes. There is also more cachet in taking overseas trips and having photo-ops with world leaders than trying to get ministries to do their job. That is why ministers often spend more time abroad than in the country, with prime ministers exceeding their predecessors’ record of foreign visits. Fixing the country’s problems is much harder than flying off to, say, Davos. A cynical explanation is that the country’s problems — poverty, hunger, lack of education, and health facilities, malnutrition, growing population numbers — don’t affect the power elite, so if they fester there is no skin off its back. Certainly, it sees no urgency in addressing them. Pakistan’s future will be determined at home, not abroad. The excessive attention that much of Pakistan’s broadcast media devotes to foreign policy and external developments is explained by other factors. The obvious one is the electronic media simply covers what the country’s leadership is doing. But it also means it is content to play follow-my-leader and not set its own agenda that takes public issues into account. Discussing foreign trips and events involves far less effort than delving into complex domestic issues. Confrontations between the government and opposition do get plenty of coverage. But when a report on an aspect of Pakistan’s economic and social situation is published, the coverage and discussion are fleeting and shallow, with no analysis or follow-up. There are occasional exceptions but an in-depth analysis or investigative documentary on a consequential socioeconomic issue is hard to come by. Above all, TV channels seem to believe serving up formulaic talk shows is enough for viewers. Yet issues that warrant the attention of primarily the government, that can do something about them, and media, which can encourage authorities to pay attention, have become even more urgent. Improving the living conditions of people is the government’s most important task. That it has not lived up to this task is apparent from the fact that poverty, for example, has risen significantly in recent years. According to the World Bank, Pakistan’s national poverty rate rose from 22 per cent in 2018-19 to 29pc in 2024-25. The WB also estimates that Pakistan accounts for almost half of the poor in the 23 countries of the MENAAP region (Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan, and Pakistan). UNDP estimates 38.3pc of Pakistan’s population face multidimensional poverty, which measures multiple, overlapping deprivations in education, health, and standard of living that go beyond a purely monetary standard of poverty. So why is the government unable to deal with the increasing number of people living below the poverty line? It is argued that the government is constrained by the macroeconomic situation and an IMF programme that is contractionary, and has to focus on stabilising the economy. But that should not prevent it from addressing poverty. There is much that can be done to reduce poverty that has nothing to do with the spending cycle. After all, the IMF hardly prevents the government from allocating resources judiciously, mobilising revenue, pursuing non-tax filers, and curbing electricity theft. Stabilising the economy has nothing to do with vanity projects undertaken at the expense of helping the poor. Poverty is also reflected in the alarming state of hunger in the country. Pakistan is among the world’s 10 countries where millions face acute hunger, according to an international humanitarian organisation, Action Against Hunger. Another recent report, No Security Without Food Security, finds Pakistan is worst hit by hunger in South Asia. Deteriorating food insecurity is attributed to economic instability, inflation, and climate shocks. Malnutrition associated with poverty is also responsible for child stunting. Around 40pc of Pakistani children under five are stunted, which condemns them to a life of physical disability, poverty, and lifelong deprivation. No issue matters more to the country’s future than education. Yet it barely gets priority attention from the government. Pakistan still has the world’s second highest number of out-of-school children, around 25m (aged five to 16) — over half of them girls. This is a national scandal. Literacy remains stagnant, with 37pc of people illiterate. No country can make economic progress with that level of illiteracy. Without investment in people, economic growth will remain elusive. The education deficit is all the more serious given the youth bulge. Over two-thirds of the population are below age 30. The young will determine the country’s destiny. But if they are uneducated and unemployable, they face a hopeless future. This jeopardises the country’s prospects. Also disturbing is the share of youth (15-29 years) who are not in education, employment, and training, known as the NEET rate, which is 37pc overall and 62pc for women, according to a Gallup report. Human capital and human development, crucial for economic growth, have suffered from government indifference and deteriorated over time. Foreign engagements count for little when there is no improvement in the condition of the majority of people. Nor does the ‘glamour’ of foreign trips obscure the grim reality of the economic and social deprivations people face across the country. Nation-building at home should have priority. Pakistan’s future, after all, will be determined at home, not abroad. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN. Published in Dawn, November 9th, 2026

items.title: Is BoG squeezing jobs to tame inflation? – Oppong Nkrumah questions policy stance
items.description: The Ranking Member of Parliament for the Economy and Development Committee, Kojo Oppong Nkrumah, has questioned whether the Bank of Ghana’s efforts to lower inflation are putting unnecessary pressure on businesses, job creation, and economic growth. During an engagement with central bank officials, he argued that monetary policy should look beyond headline inflation and consider the difficulties facing households and businesses. Mr Oppong Nkrumah pointed to the October 2026 inflation rate of 5.5%, below the Bank’s target range of 6% to 10%. He questioned whether pursuing inflation below that range risked keeping monetary conditions too restrictive. He said the inflation target should support an environment conducive to growth and employment, rather than serve solely as a statistical benchmark. A Bank of Ghana official rejected the suggestion that the central bank was deliberately pushing inflation below its target band. The official said the Bank’s forecasts showed inflation gradually returning to 8%, plus or minus two percentage points. The Monetary Policy Committee also needed to remain alert to emerging risks. Mr Oppong Nkrumah further questioned whether demand-reduction measures were appropriate when much of Ghana’s inflationary pressure was cost-driven. Citing the International Monetary Fund’s latest review, he argued that production costs, utility charges and rent required attention alongside monetary policy. He questioned whether liquidity sterilisation and other demand-management measures could constrain economic activity without directly addressing those pressures. The MP asked whether the central bank was advising the government and relevant institutions on measures to tackle rising business and household costs. In response, the BoG official said monetary policy is primarily a demand-management tool and cannot directly address supply-side pressures. The official said policy decisions were guided by economic data and balanced price stability and growth. The official also cited a reduction in the policy rate from 28% to 14% as evidence of efforts to balance inflation control with support for economic activity. Mr Oppong Nkrumah also raised concerns about differences between national inflation and the rates recorded across regions and sectors. Against the headline rate of 5.5%, he cited inflation of approximately 9.8% in the Ashanti Region and services inflation of about 8.3%. He questioned whether those differences helped explain why many people continued to experience pressure from rising living costs despite the decline in national inflation. He argued that economic indicators must be considered alongside the actual costs confronting households and businesses, particularly for essential services.

items.title: Year-round farming key to cutting food imports – Agric Minister
items.description: Agriculture Minister Eric Opoku says Ghana must expand irrigation and support year-round farming to boost food production and reduce dependence on imports. Speaking during a visit to Gyidiman Farms in Odumasua-Noahkrom, in the Afram Plains South District, he said reliance on rainfall continues to limit the country’s agricultural potential. “We have to transition Ghana’s agriculture from rainfed agriculture to irrigation agriculture,” he emphasised. The farm, led by 2025 National Best Farmer Abraham Kwaku Adusei and backed by the Saviour Church of Ghana, illustrates both the opportunities in large-scale agriculture and the challenges confronting producers. Its operations include 350 acres of cashew, 320 acres of mango and 450 acres of maize. It also produces rice, beans, and vegetables, and cultivates teak and raises livestock. Operating for more than 20 years, the farm engages thousands of workers in batches, providing employment for surrounding communities. However, inadequate rainfall has caused substantial losses. Nana Abraham said more than 500 acres of beans were affected last year. About 200 acres are currently under cultivation. “We had a difficult period last year because, due to lack of rain, we suffered a loss of over 500 acres of beans cultivated,” he recounted. He welcomed government support for an irrigation system that would draw water from the Afram River, more than 12 miles away. Mr Opoku said the procurement process for the irrigation project was nearing completion, with the Ghana Irrigation Development Authority handling the technical arrangements. He added that contractors were working to extend electricity to the farm, with completion expected by the end of December 2026. Transport difficulties remain another obstacle. Delays at the Afram River ferry crossing affect the movement of workers and produce, sometimes contributing to post-harvest losses. The minister said a contract had been awarded for a bridge project and the contractor was on site. Ongoing road construction is also expected to improve access to the farming area. Under the Feed Ghana Programme, the government is encouraging churches to participate in food production. The Saviour Church became the first church to register under the initiative. Mr Opoku said the government had supplied the church with 1,000 bags of fertiliser this year. He said the allocation could increase to match the scale of its operations. The ministry is also developing a farmer service centre to provide machinery and grain storage. Gyidiman Farms already operates a rice processing facility to add value to its produce. The minister said local and foreign investors had expressed interest in acquiring thousands of hectares for farming. He believes such investment could expand production and create jobs, particularly for young people. He urged Ghanaians to buy locally produced food to support farmers and encourage further investment. “If we have 10 Gyidiman Farms in Ghana, it will end our imports,” he said. Nana Abraham, 83 and a farmer for more than 50 years, also encouraged young people to consider careers in agriculture. “Farming is something so valuable. I’m 83 years old, and I’m still a farmer,” he said.

items.title: Ghana nears finish line in external debt restructuring – GSDR
items.description: Ghana’s external debt restructuring is nearing completion, with 16 of 25 bilateral agreements with official creditors finalised, according to the Global Sovereign Debt Roundtable (GSDR). The report, released on the sidelines of the Annual IMF–World Bank Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, said negotiations were continuing with Ghana’s remaining non-bonded commercial creditors. These creditors now account for less than 5% of the debt covered by the restructuring exercise. The bilateral agreements involve members of Ghana’s Official Creditor Committee (OCC). Completing them marks further progress toward implementing the country’s debt treatment arrangements. The GSDR brings together debtor countries and official and private creditors to improve understanding of debt sustainability and sovereign debt restructuring challenges. Launched in February 2023, the forum also seeks to identify ways to address obstacles that delay restructuring processes. Background Ghana announced a suspension of payments on selected external debts in December 2022 as part of efforts to restructure its obligations and secure support from the International Monetary Fund. The suspension covered Eurobonds, commercial loans and selected bilateral debts. Ghana established an Official Creditor Committee on May 12, 2023, to coordinate the restructuring of its bilateral debt under the G20 Common Framework. Financing assurances from creditors helped pave the way for approval of Ghana’s US$3 billion IMF programme. The programme’s approval was followed by an initial disbursement of US$600 million. The latest GSDR assessment indicates that the process has advanced substantially, with attention now focused on concluding outstanding agreements and resolving claims involving remaining commercial creditors. Concerns The report said restructuring cases had continued to progress since April 2026. These include Ethiopia, Ghana and Zambia under the Common Framework, as well as Sri Lanka and Suriname outside it. Apart from Ethiopia, where a bond exchange remained pending, the report said outstanding creditor negotiations in these cases involved only residual commercial creditors. It also noted progress in implementing agreements with official bilateral creditors. Since April, the report said, 22 new bilateral agreements had been signed across the restructuring cases. The report said the Paris Club website tracks implementation through updates.

items.title: Hitler’s ‘retreat’ sparks debate over Germany’s past and present
items.description: PERCHED on a ridge high in the German Alps lie the burned-out ruins of a mountain house frequented by Adolf Hitler, which is now at the heart of an intense debate about Germany’s Nazi past. Called The Eagle’s Nest, or Kehlsteinhaus in German, the retreat was built by the Nazis in 1938. After World War II it was classified as a historical monument. But after it was gutted in a suspected arson attack last month, some believe it is time for the site to be completely destroyed, so it can shed the mantle of its Nazi past, BBC News reported . Others, however, want it either partially or completely rebuilt, wary of the risk of turning it into a lightning rod for neo-Nazi elements at a time when Germany is witnessing the resurgence of the far-right. Before it was burned down on Oct 23, the Eagle’s Nest had been a popular tourist attraction, owned by the state of Bavaria and operating for many years as a restaurant. Visitors would take a bus and then ride the original brass and mirror-panelled lift through the mountain to the Kehlsteinhaus to savour the magnificent views above the town of Berchtesgaden. Unlike Hitler’s nearby summer residence, the Berghof, which was bombed in World War II and demolished in 1952, the Eagle’s Nest survived the war. In the 1990s, amid concerns that the site did not do enough to confront the crimes of the Nazi past, a museum, the Obersalzberg Documentation Centre, was opened close by. Although the Eagle’s Nest itself was “largely destroyed” by the fire, according to police, the documentation centre survived unscathed. The authorities have not commented on a possible motive, but a 33-year-old man with a history of mental illness has been detained on suspicion of arson. According to BBC News, some feel that this is an opportune moment to allow the site to fade into history. “It’s been torched now. It’s been destroyed. I think they should just clear away the rubble and leave the mountain as it should be in its natural state,” said Prof Sir Richard J. Evans, a specialist in Nazi Germany at the University of Cambridge. That has happened with “quite a few other Nazi sites”, he argued, including the bunker in Berlin where Hitler killed himself. But Bavaria’s authorities take a different view about the site’s future. Both the state’s interior minister, Joachim Herrmann, and its minister for the arts, Markus Blume, have spoken out in favour of rebuilding the Kehlsteinhaus. Germany and Austria have long struggled to deal with the fraught legacy of buildings and sites connected to the Nazi era. With the recent rise of the far-right AfD and the Austrian Freedom Party, the debate over Erinnerungskultur (Culture of Remembrance) has taken on a new urgency. A row broke out recently in Germany when AfD and conservative CDU councillors in a town in Saxony decided to ban “stumbling stones” memorials – embedded small brass plaques in the streets - to victims of the Nazis. In Austria over the summer, a police station was opened in the house where Hitler was born in Braunau am Inn. It followed years of controversy about how the house should be used. The Austrian government said the police presence would help prevent neo-Nazi ‘pilgrims’. But others want the site to become a centre of responsibility, actively confronting the Nazi past. Published in Dawn, November 9th, 2026

items.title: Cruise ship pianist rescued from sea after nine hours in Pacific Ocean
items.description: A cruise ship pianist was found treading water around 20 miles (32km) off the Californian coast after falling overboard, according to US media reports. Two fishermen discovered the Royal Caribbean employee near Catalina Island on Friday and officials believe he may have been in the Pacific Ocean for nine hours, according to CBS News, the BBC’s US news partner. “I’m like, ‘Yeah, it’s a human being. Stop the boat; let’s get all of our lines in,” Grant Garrett was quoted as saying, recalling the moment he and Sean Norton spotted him. The man, who has not yet been identified, was taken to hospital in a stable condition, the US Coast Guard told the BBC, adding it was investigating the incident. The fishermen say the man identified himself as a pianist on a 14-deck cruise ship called the Ovation of the Seas. “The only thing he said to me was, ‘Thank you. I thought I was gonna die,'” Norton said. The Coast Guard said in a statement it had received a report from “a Good Samaritan who recovered a conscious individual from the water”. The person was handed over to Newport Beach Lifeguards, who confirmed he was an employee of the Ovation of the Seas cruise ship, it said. Lifeguard officials believe he may have fallen overboard at around 02:30, about nine hours before he was discovered. “It was approximately 15 to 20 miles offshore, pretty much in the middle of the ocean,” Newport Beach Lifeguard Battalion Chief Adam Yacenda told CBS. Norton credited the man’s survival to unusually warm ocean temperatures. “You have this crazy super El Niño year. This guy was in the water for probably 10 hours, but the water’s 76 degrees,” Norton said, which equates to about 24C. “A different year, no way he makes it,” Norton said. The developing El Niño climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record, according to scientists monitoring the Pacific, with ocean temperatures about 3.05C above average. In a statement to the BBC, a Royal Caribbean Group spokesperson said: “We are providing support and assistance to our crew member during this difficult time. “To respect the privacy of our employee, we have no additional details to share.”

items.title: Fidelity Bank picks Atta Yeboah Gyan as MD, pending BoG approval
items.description: Fidelity Bank’s Board has selected Deputy Managing Director Atta Yeboah Gyan as the bank’s next Managing Director, effective November 21, 2026. JoyBusiness understands that the appointment is subject to regulatory approval from the Bank of Ghana (BoG). Mr Gyan is expected to succeed Julian Opuni, whose eight-year tenure as Managing Director ends on November 21. Who is Atta Yeboah Gyan? Mr Gyan has more than two decades of banking experience spanning finance, corporate strategy, risk management, operations, audit and regulatory compliance. He joined Fidelity Bank in 2007 and has held several senior positions, including Chief Financial Officer. As Deputy Managing Director, he has overseen operations and support functions. He began his banking career as an Inspector at SG-SSB, now Société Générale Ghana, after a stint at Ghana Airways. At SG-SSB, he served on an operations and control task force that supported the bank’s transition from local control to foreign ownership. Before joining Fidelity Bank, Mr Gyan worked as Finance Manager at Joy FM. He established the station’s finance function, coordinated strategy and budgeting, and oversaw credit control and client service. He is a certified Financial Risk Manager and a member of the Global Association of Risk Professionals in the United States. He is also a Chartered Accountant and a member of the Institute of Chartered Accountants, Ghana. Mr Gyan holds an Executive MBA in Finance and a Bachelor of Science in Administration, specialising in Accounting, from the University of Ghana. His qualifications also include a post-chartered diploma in International Financial Reporting Standards. Why is the board appointing a new MD now? The leadership change follows the completion of Mr Opuni’s eight-year tenure as Managing Director. Industry figures have credited him with maintaining discipline and building on the foundations laid by his predecessors. JoyBusiness understands that Mr Opuni is expected to remain available for about six months to support the transition.

items.title: Antalya agenda
items.description: WHEN COP31 opens in Antalya today, governments will have to show that years of climate negotiations have produced more than ambitious targets and promises of financial help. Geopolitical tensions, an energy crisis, and strained finances in rich countries have dampened hopes of a breakthrough. The absence of an official US delegation after Washington’s withdrawal from the Paris Agreement has worsened matters. Meanwhile, the climate crisis is advancing faster than efforts to contain it. A new UN report warns that even if countries fulfil existing climate pledges, global temperatures could rise by 2.6°C this century. For Pakistan, already exposed to floods, extreme heat, and erratic rainfall, the question is what it can realistically secure from the talks. At COP29, developed countries committed to mobilising $300bn annually for developing nations by 2035. COP30 called for progress towards a broader goal of $1.3tr a year and for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035. But promises of more money mean little if vulnerable states cannot access it. For Pakistan, the priority should be to secure easier access to climate funds, more grants rather than debt-creating loans, and clear deadlines for financial contributions. It should seek support for practical measures to protect homes from flooding, secure water supplies, and improve early warning systems. By joining forces with other vulnerable countries, Pakistan could strengthen calls for better glacier monitoring, flood protection, and affordable climate technology. Its latest climate plan aims to cut projected emissions by 50pc by 2035, with 17 percentage points unconditional and the remaining 33 reliant on international support. This gives Pakistan grounds to seek investment in cleaner energy, transport, and agriculture. But it must also pursue reforms at home, while pressing for stronger global action to reduce emissions. Pakistan’s preparations for COP31 offer an opportunity to put these priorities into practice. Its planned pavilion sessions in Antalya cover disaster preparedness, solar electrification, local adaptation, and climate investment projects. These discussions should lead to partnerships and investment proposals. Islamabad should identify priority projects and report publicly on commitments secured and money received. Provincial governments must be involved, as irrigation, land use, drainage, and emergency services are largely their responsibility. Local communities should help determine which projects receive priority funding. Pakistan must also address problems that international aid alone cannot solve, including construction on floodplains and poor enforcement of environmental rules. COP31 may produce modest advances rather than a sweeping agreement. But Pakistan can still make progress by presenting workable proposals and showing that the assistance it receives will benefit those most at risk. Published in Dawn, November 9th, 2026

items.title: After midterm rout, Vance tries to build his own 2028 brand
items.description: Late in his blitz to salvage Republicans’ midterm fortunes , Vice President JD Vance shifted strategy. He talked less about President Donald Trump and more about the issues that define his own political identity. Vance argued the case ​for Republicans, who lost control of Congress in Tuesday’s vote, almost exclusively through the lens of his policy portfolio, according to a Reuters review of half a dozen speeches since the ‌Republican convention in September. He bypassed Trump’s signature policies, including the Iran war and deportations, as polls showed the president’s sagging popularity dragging down Republican office-seekers. The change was deliberate, according to two people familiar with the strategy. Vance and his advisers saw the issues he championed — economic nationalism, foreign policy restraint, and public safety — as politically potent subjects he could address with authority. While Trump embraced them as part of his MAGA movement, people said Vance had emerged as their lead crusader. The shift offered an early glimpse of ​how the 42-year-old vice president could chart his own course as Republicans begin looking beyond Trump. Vance hasn’t said whether he will run for president in 2028, and Trump hasn’t endorsed him or anyone else. ​But Vance is viewed as a leading potential contender who some Republican officials say will need to inherit much of Trump’s coalition while separating himself from his boss’s ⁠baggage. Vance took a more public step on Wednesday toward reinforcing his own political brand with an unusually blunt election postmortem. In a social media post , he blamed the Iran war for Republicans’ midterm defeat and laid out a ​platform for a Republican rebound. He called for a swift end to the conflict and urged Republicans to focus on affordability, reevaluate foreign relations and overhaul the US relationship with Israel. Trump has called Americans’ affordability concerns a Democratic “hoax.” He ​launched a war against Iran following sustained lobbying from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu . Trump went on to endorse Netanyahu in the Israeli election. VANCE MAKES UNEASE AT THE WAR PUBLIC The post for the first time put Vance openly on the side of ending the war. Three people familiar with the White House and Vance’s communications told Reuters that the vice president was not breaking with Trump and said White House chief of staff Susie Wiles knew in advance about Vance’s post. On Friday, Trump reshuffled senior White House leadership , replacing ​Wiles with Stephen Miller in a move that suggests the White House plans to double down on some of Trump’s more hardline policies. Trump has acknowledged the Iran war played a role in the Republican rout because of the ​resulting high gas prices but has continued to defend it. “I would have done nothing different,” he told reporters on Wednesday. Reuters could not determine whether Trump knew about the post in advance. Donald Trump Jr., the president’s eldest son, endorsed Vance’s remarks ‌on social media, ⁠along with some conservative allies. The dialogue further elevated Vance as a potential post-Trump conservative standard-bearer, said Michael Ricci, a Republican strategist and former adviser to House Speakers John Boehner and Paul Ryan. USING THE MEGAPHONE OF THE VICE PRESIDENCY He said Vance’s message forced conservatives to debate the merits of the war, and more broadly, what core tenets Republican presidential candidates should embrace in 2028. “It’s simplistic to say this about him looking for ways to differentiate himself from Trump,” Ricci said. “This is about him using his megaphone of the vice presidency to set the terms of debate.” Representatives for Vance declined to comment. White House representatives referred Reuters to Trump’s comments on Wednesday, when he told reporters he understood ​Vance’s perspective on the election results. Democrats are poised to ​tie Vance – or any Republican nominee – to Trump ⁠in 2028, especially if Trump plays a large role in vetting conservative hopefuls. “There’s a real challenge of how you position yourself to be viable in a general election while winning a primary that still requires you to bow down and kiss the ring,” said Igor Volsky, a Democratic strategist. Vance’s brand did not emerge from the midterms unscathed. ​Republicans lost in states where he campaigned. Some of the strategies he endorsed – including an ad by Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy that cast doubt on the ​sexual abuse suffered by the ⁠victorious Democratic candidate, Amy Acton – may have swung races away from Republicans. Other possible 2028 presidential contenders have offered their diagnoses of the midterm defeat. Texas Senator Ted Cruz said Republicans hadn’t done enough on affordability. Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said losing candidates had focused too heavily on transgender issues and neglected voter concerns about data centres and artificial intelligence. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has stayed silent. Vance’s effort to shape the debate was visible in the campaign’s closing days. In stump ​speeches, he told voters to support Republicans because they would investigate fraud in federal health care and antipoverty programs, tying that to the ​White House’s immigration agenda and cost of living. He almost entirely ignored the Iran war and gas prices, and seldom mentioned Trump by name. “I want my kids to raise a family in a country that is vibrant and thriving and free and prosperous. I want the ​simple things,” Vance told one of his final rallies in North Carolina. “And because I want that for me, I want it for you too.”

items.description: President Donald Trump will meet with Qatar’s prime minister at the White House on Monday, ​according to the White House schedule, as the ‌conflict with Iran drags on and diplomatic efforts to end it face significant obstacles. Trump is due to meet with Sheikh ​Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, who also serves as ​Qatar’s foreign minister, in a closed-door meeting. ⁠Vice President JD Vance is also scheduled to ​meet with the Qatari leader, according to a US ​official. Qatar has played a central role as an intermediary between Washington and Tehran, conveying proposals and seeking to bridge ​differences over Iran’s nuclear program and the terms ​for ending the conflict. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Sunday ‌that ⁠negotiations with Iran had made little progress and that he did not see an imminent breakthrough. Speaking before departing Florida for a G7 foreign ministers meeting ​in Paris, ​Rubio said ⁠Trump preferred a diplomatic solution but described Iran’s demands as “unacceptable” and, in some ​cases, “outrageous and ridiculous, and really not ​realistic.” Trump said ⁠Sunday that he was highly unlikely to order new strikes against Iran if negotiations made progress and produced a ⁠strong ​agreement, but warned that the ​United States had identified additional infrastructure targets, including bridges, should military ​action resume.

items.title: Mexican expert: CPC discipline key to sustaining long-term governance
items.description: The Communist Party of China (CPC) has consistently upheld strict organizational discipline and unity as cornerstones of its development and governance since its founding in 1921, said Ehecatl Lazaro, a researcher at the Mexican Center for Economic and Social Studies and a specialist in China studies. The CPC has also remained committed to its long-term goal of achieving socialist modernization, Lazaro said in an interview with CGTN. He contrasted the CPC's approach with that of Mexico's Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), attributing the latter's eventual loss of power in part to weak internal discipline and a lack of organizational cohesion. Founded in 1929, the PRI governed Mexico for 71 consecutive years, from 1929 to 2000, making it the longest-ruling political party in Latin American history. Despite its decades in power, the PRI eventually lost its grip on government, said Lazaro, adding that corruption and a lack of strict internal party discipline were decisive factors in its decline. The PRI's experience highlights the importance of organizational discipline and internal unity in sustaining a political party's cohesion and long-term governance, Lazaro said.

items.title: IA : à force de déléguer notre réflexion, risquons-nous d’affaiblir notre cerveau ?
items.description: Rédiger un courriel, résumer un document, trouver une idée ou prendre une décision : l’intelligence artificielle s’impose progressivement dans les gestes du quotidien. Mais cette facilité croissante pourrait avoir un coût sur nos capacités cognitives et nos relations sociales, met en garde le neuroscientifique David Rock. L’intelligence artificielle est devenue un outil du quotidien. En quelques secondes, elle peut produire un texte, synthétiser un rapport, répondre à une question ou proposer des pistes de réflexion. Un gain de temps considérable, qui transforme déjà les habitudes de travail et d’accès à l’information. Mais cette délégation croissante de tâches intellectuelles soulève une interrogation : que se passe-t-il lorsque nous cessons progressivement de solliciter notre propre cerveau ? C’est le point d’attention soulevé par le neuroscientifique David Rock, cofondateur et directeur général du NeuroLeadership Institute. Selon lui, le débat ne devrait pas se limiter aux performances des nouvelles technologies, mais porter aussi sur leurs effets sur nos comportements et nos capacités de réflexion. Le cerveau humain conserve ses mécanismes fondamentaux, explique-t-il, mais les changements technologiques et les nouvelles habitudes qu’ils entraînent peuvent modifier profondément notre manière de travailler, de décider et d’interagir. Le risque de laisser l’IA réfléchir à notre place Pour David Rock, neuroscientifique et cofondateur du NeuroLeadership Institute, le principal paradoxe de l’intelligence artificielle réside dans la facilité qu’elle procure. Trouver une information, organiser une tâche ou obtenir une première réponse ne demande désormais que quelques secondes. Cette disponibilité permanente peut libérer du temps, mais elle encourage aussi le recours systématique à des solutions immédiates. Le neuroscientifique observe que seule une minorité de travailleurs, estimée entre 5 et 10 %, utiliserait pleinement ces outils pour automatiser les tâches répétitives et consacrer davantage de temps aux activités qui nécessitent réflexion et créativité. Une majorité risquerait, au contraire, de leur confier une part croissante de son travail intellectuel. « Le cerveau adore économiser de l’énergie », rappelle-t-il. La tentation de ne plus fournir d’effort devient alors importante, avec un risque de diminution progressive des capacités d’analyse et de jugement lorsque les individus délèguent à la machine non seulement l’exécution, mais aussi l’évaluation et la prise de décision. Pour David Rock, il est donc essentiel de maintenir une activité intellectuelle régulière. « Si votre cerveau n’est plus sollicité, vous perdez très vite ces compétences », avertit il. Une attention mise à rude épreuve Cette évolution intervient alors que les capacités de concentration sont déjà fortement sollicitées. Courriels, notifications, messages, mises à jour et contenus générés par l’IA alimentent un flux continu d’informations, dont le volume dépasse souvent ce qu’un individu peut traiter efficacement. Le problème n’est plus seulement d’accéder à l’information, mais de parvenir à la sélectionner, à la comprendre et à lui donner du sens. David Rock rappelle que le cerveau humain dispose de limites réelles, contrairement aux systèmes informatiques capables de traiter simultanément d’importantes quantités de données. Il compare cette période aux débuts de l’automobile, lorsque les usages de la voiture se sont développés avant que les règles de circulation et les limitations de vitesse ne soient pleinement établies. Selon lui, l’adoption de l’intelligence artificielle progresse plus rapidement que les garde-fous collectifs nécessaires à son utilisation. Quand les machines investissent le champ des relations humaines Les effets de l’IA ne concernent pas uniquement le travail ou la concentration. David Rock s’inquiète également de la place prise par les agents conversationnels dans la vie personnelle. De plus en plus d’utilisateurs les sollicitent pour discuter, obtenir des conseils ou rechercher une forme de compagnie. Il estime que ces outils touchent à des mécanismes humains liés à l’attachement et aux relations sociales. Certaines recherches qu’il évoque suggèrent que les personnes qui interagissent intensivement avec des compagnons artificiels peuvent ressentir davantage de solitude, tandis que d’autres travaux font état d’un lien entre l’usage important des agents conversationnels et le recul des échanges sociaux réels. Cette évolution pose la question de la place des interactions humaines dans un environnement où les machines peuvent désormais simuler une conversation et répondre de manière personnalisée. Pour le neuroscientifique, les relations sociales restent essentielles au développement et au fonctionnement du cerveau. La relation humaine, une valeur appelée à compter davantage À mesure que les systèmes artificiels deviennent capables de produire des contenus, d’analyser des données et d’imiter des échanges, les qualités propres aux relations humaines pourraient gagner en importance. David Rock met notamment en avant la confiance, l’authenticité et la qualité des liens entre les individus. « L’expérience humaine va acquérir une valeur bien plus grande », estime-t-il. Cette évolution pourrait conduire à une nouvelle appréciation des relations professionnelles et personnelles, dans lesquelles la collaboration, le sens et la confiance conserveraient une place centrale, même face à des outils technologiques toujours plus performants. Préserver la maîtrise de sa propre réflexion Pour faire face à ces mutations, David Rock met en avant la métacognition, c’est-à-dire la capacité à observer et à comprendre ses propres mécanismes de pensée. L’enjeu n’est pas de se détourner de l’intelligence artificielle, mais d’apprendre à l’utiliser sans lui abandonner le contrôle de son raisonnement. Les outils peuvent aider à confronter des idées, tester des hypothèses, explorer d’autres interprétations ou élargir les perspectives. Mais l’analyse et le jugement final doivent rester humains. Le neuroscientifique résume cette approche par le principe de « primauté de l’humain ». L’intelligence artificielle peut ainsi devenir un appui à la réflexion, à condition de ne pas s’y substituer. Dans un environnement où les technologies évoluent à un rythme accéléré, préserver sa capacité à analyser, à décider et à entretenir des relations réelles apparaît comme l’un des principaux défis des prochaines années. Comme le souligne David Rock, « le changement n’a jamais été aussi rapide », mais « il ne sera plus jamais aussi lent ». items.title: Tanzanian opposition leader cleared of treason, sentenced for incitement
items.description: Tanzania’s main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu , was cleared ​of treason but convicted of incitement and sentenced to four years in jail on Friday, in a case that rights groups and ‌his supporters say is politically motivated. Police surrounded the courtroom in the commercial capital Dar es Salaam and crowds gathered nearby as authorities brought Lissu to the hearing in a heavily guarded convoy. The chairperson of Tanzania’s biggest opposition party, CHADEMA, was arrested in April last year. Protests over ​his detention and other grievances escalated into the worst political unrest in the country’s history during elections in October 2025. HUNDREDS ​DIED IN PROTESTS The charge related to a speech Lissu gave that April when prosecutors say he told ⁠supporters that the opposition would “block the election” and “mobilise rebellion”. He pleaded not guilty, arguing during the trial that his speech ​did not violate any law and that the charges were politically motivated. The government has dismissed accusations of a crackdown ​on dissent and said protesters started the violence. Video posted on CHADEMA’s X account on Friday showed Lissu being escorted to the court by guards, some masked. He was seen waving his fist in the air briefly and shouting “Do not fear!” in Swahili. More clips from CHADEMA showed Lissu in ​the dock, sporting dreadlocks with a blue rosary around his left arm, waving to people inside the packed courtroom ​and shouting “We will arrive”. They were seen responding “Yes” in Swahili. Lissu planned to appeal against the jail sentence, his party’s spokesperson, Brenda Rupia, told Reuters. Rugemeleza ‌Nshala, CHADEMA’s ⁠chief legal counsel, told reporters that he would also apply for bail in the meantime. Amnesty International said the guilty verdict was a travesty of justice and called for Lissu’s release. “Tundu Lissu should never have been arrested, let alone prosecuted and convicted,” Tigere Chagutah, the group’s regional director for East and Southern Africa, said. Lissu’s detention, along with CHADEMA’s disqualification from ​the vote and allegations by ​rights groups that government critics ⁠were abducted, was a key driver of protests that broke out during last year’s elections. Hundreds died as police opened fire on protesters in multiple cities, undermining the country’s longstanding ​reputation for stability. A commission appointed by President Samia Suluhu Hassan said in April that at ​least 518 people ⁠were killed in the violence, which it blamed on protesters. Her government denied allegations by human rights groups that the security services used excessive force. She was declared winner of the election with nearly 98% of the vote. The US ambassador to Tanzania, ⁠William ​Trachman, wrote on X on Thursday that he was closely following the ​trial and its “broader implications for the rule of law”. The US government said last December it was reviewing its relationship with Tanzania due to violence against ​civilians and other concerns.

items.title: Bouré-Balato : une bagarre entre travailleuses du sexe fait une blessée grave dans un maquis surnommé « Nigéria »
items.description: Un violent affrontement a éclaté jeudi dernier dans un maquis situé dans la haute banlieue de Bouré-Balato, dans Siguiri, communément appelé « Nigéria ». Cet établissement de loisirs, ainsi surnommé en raison de la forte présence de travailleuses du sexe de nationalité nigériane, a été le théâtre d’une altercation sur fond de rivalité professionnelle et de jalousie. Une personne a été grièvement blessée à la tête. Voici le déroulement des faits, selon les informations recueillies par notre correspondant à Kintinian, à l’issue d’investigations menées sur le terrain et clôturées dimanche soir. Selon plusieurs témoignages recueillis, le conflit couvait depuis un certain temps. Une jeune femme de nationalité sierra-léonaise, exerçant dans l’établissement, ferait l’objet d’une forte sollicitation de la part des clients. Une situation qui aurait alimenté la rancœur de la responsable du groupe, une ressortissante nigériane. Jeudi, jour des faits, la tension aurait atteint son paroxysme autour d’une tâche ménagère : le nettoyage du réservoir d’eau (tank) de l’établissement, une opération effectuée à tour de rôle. Bien que la jeune Sierra-Léonaise se soit acquittée de cette tâche, la responsable aurait rejeté son travail à plusieurs reprises, lui demandant de recommencer. Malgré trois tentatives de nettoyage, jugées impeccables par plusieurs témoins extérieurs sollicités pour apprécier le résultat, cette dernière aurait persisté dans ses exigences, contraignant la jeune femme à poursuivre la tâche, pendant que ses collègues commençaient déjà à recevoir leurs premiers clients de la journée. Face aux protestations de la Sierra-Léonaise, le ton serait rapidement monté. Aux insultes proférées par la responsable se seraient ajoutées celles d’autres travailleuses du sexe de nationalité nigériane, qui auraient fait bloc contre leur collègue. Une brève intervention du gérant de l’établissement aurait alors permis de calmer momentanément la situation. Celui-ci aurait donné raison à la jeune Sierra-Léonaise avant de s’absenter quelques instants. C’est durant cette absence que la situation aurait dégénéré en une agression physique collective. Seule face au groupe, la jeune femme aurait tenté de se défendre et de repousser ses assaillantes. C’est au cours de cette altercation que l’une des ressortissantes nigérianes aurait été grièvement blessée au niveau du front. Alerté en urgence par téléphone, le propriétaire du maquis, désigné sous l’appellation de PDG, un maçon de profession également employé à la SAG, s’est précipité sur les lieux. Sa tentative de transporter la blessée à l’hôpital se serait toutefois heurtée au refus catégorique de ses compatriotes, qui auraient exigé de se rendre immédiatement au poste de police pour déposer une plainte. Face à la gravité de la situation, les forces de l’ordre de Balato ont procédé à l’interpellation des protagonistes, qui ont été retenus pour les besoins de l’enquête. Interrogée par notre équipe de reporters, l’autorité policière a apporté des précisions sur la qualification juridique des faits. Selon ses explications, l’infraction officiellement retenue et enregistrée par le commissariat est celle de « coups et blessures volontaires ». Le dossier aurait été entièrement traité et réglé au niveau de cette juridiction policière, sans transmission au parquet. Pour obtenir sa libération et la réouverture de son établissement, le propriétaire du maquis aurait pris un engagement écrit de veiller à ce qu’un tel incident ne se reproduise plus. La police confirme également que les personnes impliquées dans cette bagarre ont été définitivement expulsées de l’établissement. Aux dernières nouvelles, la personne blessée au front recevait des soins médicaux et son état ne présenterait plus de danger vital. Dimanche, après la clôture de nos investigations, nous nous sommes rendus sur les lieux, dans la haute banlieue de Bouré-Balato. Le maquis avait effectivement rouvert ses portes et repris ses activités. Bien que nous n’ayons pas encore eu l’occasion de rencontrer personnellement le propriétaire, nos constatations sur le terrain semblent corroborer les mesures annoncées par les autorités : les travailleuses du sexe de nationalité nigériane auraient quitté les lieux, tandis que la ressortissante sierra-léonaise serait toujours présente dans l’établissement. Ce fait divers met en lumière une problématique préoccupante à Bouré : la multiplication des maquis dans plusieurs zones stratégiques, parfois sans encadrement suffisant. Ces établissements de loisirs, souvent implantés à proximité des zones résidentielles ou minières, peuvent devenir des lieux de tensions et d’insécurité, où se côtoient consommation d’alcool, prostitution et rivalités entre personnes de différentes nationalités. L’absence d’une réglementation suffisamment rigoureuse et d’une surveillance adaptée expose aussi bien les populations riveraines que les personnes fréquentant ces établissements à des risques de dérives et de violences. Même si cette affaire aurait trouvé une issue au niveau du commissariat de police, les événements survenus à Bouré-Balato devraient interpeller les autorités communales et préfectorales sur la nécessité de mieux encadrer l’implantation et le fonctionnement de ces lieux de loisirs, afin de préserver l’ordre public et la quiétude sociale. Affaire à suivre. Mamoudou Kéïta, correspondant à Kintinian L’article Bouré-Balato : une bagarre entre travailleuses du sexe fait une blessée grave dans un maquis surnommé « Nigéria » est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Heatwaves in Punjab threaten agriculture, food security: UN
items.description: • Report says fruit yields plunge 50pc; heat stress spreads livestock disease, cuts milk output • Shrinking incomes, food spoilage limit rural families’ healthy diets • Women bear brunt of crisis due to heavy outdoor labour; preterm birth risk jumps 26pc in severe weather ISLAMABAD: Increasingly frequent and severe heatwaves in Punjab’s rain-fed rural areas are disrupting agricultural production, reducing household incomes and worsening food insecurity, particularly among women and vulnerable communities, according to a report by United Nations (UN) agencies. The assessment “Extreme Heat and Agriculture”, was published jointly by the UN Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) and the World Meteorological Organization (WMO). It warns that rising temperatures have emerged as one of the most serious and acute hazards facing global food production, threatening the livelihoods of billions of people while inflicting immediate economic and nutritional damage on vulnerable farming communities. “The effects of extreme heat on production are stark, as heat wav­es have led to significant declines in crop yields,” the report said. In the high-rainfall zones of Punjab, fruit productivity has fallen by as much as 50 per cent, the agencies found. Livestock operations across the region are also severely affected. Large ruminants produce less milk under heat stress, and small ruminants face increased outbreaks of foot-and-mouth disease, the report said. For rural families dependent on farming, the loss of agricultural output directly translates into reduced household income and diminishes their ability to purchase basic food staples. The crisis is compounded by the accelerated spoilage of vegetables, dairy products and other perishable goods in extreme temperatures. That widespread spoilage further reduces local food availability and drives up market prices. As a result, rural families face a double burden. They produce less diverse and nutritious food for their own consumption while simultaneously losing the agricultural income they rely on to purchase food from markets. “This double burden severely limits their access to healthy diets,” the report said. Although entire communities are affected, women generally bear a disproportionate share of the burden, the UN agencies found. Women in Punjab play an essential role in agricultural activities, including harvesting, collecting water and carrying out physically demanding household responsibilities. This exposes them to high temperatures for extended periods, increasing their risk of heat-related illnesses and other health complications. Those health risks are particularly acute for pregnant and lactating women, who have greater nutritional and dietary needs that are often the first to be compromised during periods of household food scarcity. Research cited in the report indicates that each 1°C rise in temperature is associated with a 4pc increase in the likelihood of preterm birth. During heat waves, the risk of preterm birth jumps to 26pc, according to the report. Additional social inequalities exacerbate women’s vulnerabilities to extreme heat. Despite their critical role in farming, women often lack ownership of land and other assets, necessary to access credit and financial services that could aid adaptation. With limited access to climate information and early warning systems, they are often less prepared to respond to heat events. Rural women’s coping strategies, such as reducing their own food intake to prioritise other family members, which can further compromise their health and resilience, reflect broader patterns of gender discrimination that amplify their vulnerability in times of climate crisis, the report said. Beyond the localised crisis in Punjab, the FAO and the WMO warned that extreme heat is acting as a powerful risk multiplier with direct and indirect impacts across all agricultural subsectors worldwide. Rising temperatures amplify existing environmental hazards such as drought, heighten the risk of destructive wildfires and create complex compound impacts. Those converging threats endanger not only global agricultural production, but also the physical health of agricultural workers who labour on the front lines of the growing climate threat. The fingerprints of extreme heat on agriculture are already visible worldwide, and the analysis of scientific evidence confirms that heat is driving significant productivity losses. Under high-emission scenarios, nearly half the world’s cattle could be exposed to dangerous heat by 2100, with annual losses nearing $40bn, although under a low-emission scenario, impacts from livestock exposure to extreme heat are reduced by nearly two-thirds. In aquatic systems, marine heatwaves have already caused repeated mass mortality events and are forcing entire fish stocks to migrate in search of cooler water. Fruit and nut trees and natural forests are also subject to production losses and the growing risk of more frequent and intense wildfires. Together, those global agricultural losses create a dangerous environmental feedback loop, the report concluded. When heat-driven shortfalls in crop and livestock production prompt farmers to clear additional land for agricultural expansion to compensate for lost yields, the resulting land-use changes increase greenhouse gas emissions — fuelling further climate change. Published in Dawn, November 9th, 2026

items.title: 66e anniversaire de l’assassinat de Félix-Roland Moumié : Camerounais et Guinéens ravivent la flamme du panafricanisme à Conakry
items.description: À Conakry, la mémoire de Félix-Roland Moumié continue de rapprocher les peuples camerounais et guinéen. À l’occasion du 66e anniversaire de l’assassinat du héros panafricaniste camerounais, une cérémonie commémorative s’est tenue, samedi 7 novembre 2026, au cimetière de Boulbinet, à Kaloum. Une rencontre organisée autour de sa mémoire, de son combat pour l’indépendance et de son idéal d’émancipation africaine. Organisée notamment par le Mouvement révolutionnaire interafricain (MRI) et le Réseau d’Éducation citoyenne pour l’intégration et la promotion de l’excellence en Afrique (RECIPE Afrique), avec la participation de la communauté camerounaise vivant en Guinée, la cérémonie a également permis de rendre hommage à Marcel Kengué, décédé le 8 juin 2026 à Bruxelles. Au-delà du dépôt de gerbe et de l’hommage rendu au militant camerounais, les participants ont voulu inscrire cette commémoration dans une réflexion plus large sur la transmission de la mémoire, l’unité africaine et la poursuite du combat panafricaniste. Pour Saïdou Camara, président du Mouvement révolutionnaire interafricain (MRI), commémorer Félix-Roland Moumié ne revient pas simplement à se souvenir d’un homme disparu. C’est avant tout une manière de transmettre aux générations actuelles les valeurs qu’il incarnait dans son combat pour la souveraineté et l’indépendance. « Commémorer les morts, ça voudrait dire enseigner aux vivants les vertus, les sources du patriotisme. Parce qu’on ne commémore pas un mort parce qu’il était beau ou parce qu’elle était belle. On commémore une personne décédée pour assassinat parce qu’elle portait, elle incarnait quelque chose. Le docteur Félix-Roland Moumié fait partie de ceux-là qui incarnaient l’idéologie révolutionnaire et l’idéologie révolutionnaire souverainiste. Il était une personne souverainiste, un indépendantiste camerounais. Au-delà de sa formation de médecin, c’était un souverainiste qui s’est battu pendant des années pour donner de l’indépendance et de la liberté au peuple camerounais, mais qui a heurté les violences du système impérialiste qui existait au Cameroun et qui a eu raison de lui », explique-t-il. Pour le président du MRI, la disparition physique du leader camerounais n’a cependant pas mis fin à son combat. « Ils ont pris sa vie, certes, mais ils n’ont pas pu vaincre son idéal, puisque, à chaque fois que nous nous souviendrons de lui, son combat ne sera pas vain. Nous avons aussi commémoré le décès de monsieur Marcel Kengué, qui venait régulièrement en Guinée pour rendre hommage au docteur Félix-Roland Moumié, pour rendre hommage au président Ahmed Sékou Touré. Et il a travaillé avec nous », témoigne Saïdou Camara. Pour Gaël Djomo, ancien secrétaire général de l’Association des ressortissants camerounais en Guinée, cette commémoration constitue avant tout un devoir de mémoire envers celui qu’il considère comme l’un des acteurs majeurs du combat pour la libération du Cameroun. Il en profite également pour saluer l’accueil réservé par la Guinée à cette cérémonie. « C’est déjà un devoir pour nous de redevabilité, parce que nous lui devons nos libérations, nous lui devons cette édification qui nous a apportés dans la lutte, dans le sacrifice ultime de son combat. C’est aussi l’occasion pour nous de remercier le peuple guinéen et les autorités guinéennes qui ont bien voulu nous accorder ce moment de pouvoir commémorer l’assassinat odieux de cet illustre compatriote africain d’origine camerounaise », dit-il. Pour lui, cette rencontre doit également servir à raviver les relations historiques entre les deux peuples, marquées par des périodes de tensions et d’incompréhensions. « Vous savez, il y a eu beaucoup de discussions, il y a eu beaucoup d’incompréhensions entre nos États. C’étaient des moments très tendus entre le Cameroun et la Guinée sur l’idéologie qu’on pouvait se faire dans le processus d’accession à notre indépendance », rappelle Gaël Djomo. Il appelle ainsi à une nouvelle dynamique entre les deux pays : « Aujourd’hui, je pense qu’il faut que nos autorités se rencontrent, que les intellectuels camerounais et guinéens puissent se rencontrer, échanger en toute convivialité sur les dispositions qu’il faudrait mettre en place pour mieux renforcer nos relations. Aujourd’hui, cette commémoration, c’était un appel à la solidarité, c’était un appel à l’unité africaine. Et il est de bon ton que le peuple camerounais et le peuple guinéen, au plus haut niveau même, les autorités, puissent se parler pour que, enfin, on puisse voir les points communs que nous avons ensemble afin de bâtir une coopération solide entre nos deux pays », plaide-t-il. Interrogé sur la pérennité de cette commémoration, Gaël Djomo se veut rassurant. « On n’a pas cette impression quand même, parce qu’aujourd’hui, on bénéficie d’un accompagnement, surtout du côté guinéen, pour cette commémoration-là. Mais on s’est dit aussi que, du côté camerounais, il y a quand même de l’ouverture, il y a des mentalités qui ont évolué, il y a une appréhension qui a aussi évolué. Si la Guinée pose les jalons de l’unité, il faudrait bien que, ne serait-ce que les Camerounais vivant en Guinée, suivent le pas vers l’unité africaine. » Prenant part à cette cérémonie, Mohamed Touré, fils du premier président guinéen Ahmed Sékou Touré, rappelle les liens historiques qui unissent la Guinée à la mémoire de Félix-Roland Moumié. « C’est devenu pratiquement une tradition pour nous de commémorer le décès, la disparition physique du camarade Félix-Roland Moumié, centre de l’indépendance africaine et leader de la lutte de libération du peuple camerounais », souligne-t-il. Il revient également sur les circonstances de la mort de Moumié et sur le lien particulier entre cette disparition et la Guinée. « Ce décès est très lié à la Guinée puisqu’il a été l’objet d’un assassinat perfide de la part d’agents de deuxième bureau français. Son assassinat a été si perfide qu’en réalité, le montage aurait été qu’il soit empoisonné à Genève, mais qu’il vienne expirer à Conakry, pour que, après, non seulement la perte de Félix-Roland Moumié, on accuse Conakry d’avoir fait exécuter cet assassinat », rapporte Mohamed Touré. Selon lui, le parcours des combattants africains ayant trouvé refuge ou soutien en Guinée explique également la portée symbolique de cette commémoration. « Dans le processus de la lutte de libération du Cameroun, comme dans le processus de libération de beaucoup de nations africaines, des leaders, des cadres de mouvements respectifs sont venus en Guinée et beaucoup de Camerounais sont venus en Guinée », rappelle-t-il. Il voit dans la présence actuelle de ressortissants camerounais à cette cérémonie la continuité de cette histoire. « Vous avez vu aujourd’hui la salle pleine de ressortissants camerounais qui sont les descendants de ces premiers. Donc, depuis un certain nombre d’années, avec l’organisation de quelques jeunes Africains guinéens, les Camerounais fêtent tous les ans, commémorent avec nous la vie et l’œuvre de Félix Moumié », explique-t-il. Pour Mohamed Touré, le choix de la Guinée pour honorer la mémoire de Moumié n’est donc pas anodin. « Le choix apporté sur la Guinée pour cette commémoration est symbolique, puisque ça veut dire que la Guinée, palpitante de l’Afrique, a participé à la lutte de libération du Cameroun et cette lutte se perpétue jusqu’à présent. C’est le cas, de toutes les façons, de beaucoup d’autres mouvements de libération qui ont été constitués et qui ont pris parfois naissance en Guinée ou, en tout cas, qui ont connu le soutien indéfectible du peuple de Guinée à travers le parti révolutionnaire, le parti d’avant-garde africaine, le Parti démocratique de Guinée, et à la tête duquel se trouvait le responsable suprême de la Révolution démocratique africaine, le camarade Ahmed Sékou Touré », rappelle-t-il. Ancien ministre guinéen et membre du PDG-RDA, Madifing Diané insiste, lui aussi, sur la dimension historique de la cérémonie. « L’essentiel à retenir ici, c’est la fidélité d’un peuple à tous ses engagements. C’est pour commémorer la mort de Félix-Roland Moumié, président de l’Union des populations du Cameroun (UPC) », souligne-t-il. Pour lui, le combat de Moumié était indissociable de celui des autres figures de la lutte anticoloniale africaine. Il estime que cette relation dépassait les frontières du Cameroun et de la Guinée. « Roland Moumié, il a été assassiné à cause de sa conviction, à cause de son engagement pour la libération du peuple congolais, du peuple camerounais. Son amitié dans ce combat avec Ahmed Sékou Touré a amené sa dépouille ici après avoir visité ce pays de son vivant. C’est donc à travers sa mémoire que nous commémorons tous ces illustres Africains qui sont passés en Guinée. Les mouvements afro-américains, le mouvement de libération des peuples angolais, mozambicains, de Guinée-Bissau, du Cap-Vert, de Namibie, du Zimbabwe, ils sont nombreux à citer », énumère-t-il. Pour Saint-Forien Téne, écrivain, panafricaniste et président du Réseau d’Éducation citoyenne pour l’intégration et la promotion de l’excellence en Afrique (RECIPE Afrique), la principale leçon de cette commémoration reste celle de l’unité africaine. « Mais ce qu’on peut retenir, c’est l’unité africaine. Au-delà de la commémoration du 66e anniversaire de l’assassinat du docteur Félix-Roland Moumié, qui était aussi un très grand leader panafricaniste, héros du continent africain, héros du Cameroun », affirme-t-il. Il insiste sur la nécessité de maintenir vivante la mémoire des figures historiques du panafricanisme. « Nous avons célébré aujourd’hui au cimetière de Boulbinet, à Kaloum, le 66e anniversaire de son assassinat à Genève, le 3 novembre 1960. Donc, si les communautés africaines, comme vous le dites si bien, camerounaises, guinéennes et bien d’autres, se sont réunies, c’est pour honorer ce grand homme et pour porter la lutte du panafricanisme africain qu’ils nous ont laissé et que nous continuons à mener jusqu’à notre dernier souffle », déclare-t-il. S’adressant à la jeunesse, il appelle à une appropriation de cet héritage. « À la nouvelle génération, nous devons tous dire de rejoindre le combat panafricaniste et de s’engager pour continuer la lutte de nos devanciers, des pères du panafricanisme, à l’instar du feu président Ahmed Sékou Touré et du docteur Félix-Roland Moumié, et bien d’autres encore », lance Saint-Forien Téne. Mais l’écrivain estime que la transmission de cette mémoire reste confrontée à un défi majeur : l’éloignement de la jeunesse africaine de certaines références historiques. « La nouvelle génération aujourd’hui en Afrique est presque en perte de repères. Ça, il faut le dire très honnêtement, parce qu’on a de la peine à la rassembler autour des événements comme ceux-ci, où elle doit venir s’abreuver auprès des sages, des vieux et de la génération intermédiaire que nous sommes, pour prendre le relais de ce combat pour la libération totale de l’Afrique », regrette-t-il. Il formule alors un message à l’endroit de la jeunesse africaine : « Panafricaniste, c’est tout simplement dire à tous les Africains et à tous les amoureux de l’Afrique de s’engager dans le combat panafricaniste, de penser africain, de rêver africain, de prier africain, de faire un retour aux sources pour pouvoir se projeter dans le futur et porter l’Afrique au firmament du monde entier. » Pour les organisateurs, les prochaines éditions devront également bénéficier d’une mobilisation accrue des autorités, de la jeunesse et des médias. « Aux autorités guinéennes, nous exhortons un accompagnement beaucoup plus appuyé pour que les éditions suivantes soient de grandes réussites, afin de transmettre la mémoire de nos vaillants combattants de la liberté aux générations futures. Pour la commémoration à venir, les attentes sont simplement un appui du gouvernement de la République de Guinée, une forte mobilisation de la jeunesse et aussi une meilleure représentativité des médias que vous êtes, parce qu’on n’a pas vu assez de médias à cette commémoration-là. Nous déplorons ce fait parce que les médias que vous êtes, vous êtes les relais de ce genre d’événement pour toucher le maximum de jeunes qui, comme je le disais tout à l’heure, sont en perte de vitesse et en perte de repères », estime-t-il. Au fil des témoignages, la cérémonie de Conakry aura ainsi dépassé le simple cadre d’un anniversaire historique. Elle a servi de trait d’union entre deux peuples liés par une histoire commune, celle des luttes anticoloniales et des aspirations à la souveraineté. Soixante-six ans après l’assassinat de Félix-Roland Moumié, son nom continue donc d’être associé, en Guinée comme au Cameroun, à un idéal que les participants entendent transmettre aux générations futures : celui d’une Afrique souveraine, solidaire et capable de construire ses propres voies de développement et d’émancipation. Mayi Cissé L’article 66e anniversaire de l’assassinat de Félix-Roland Moumié : Camerounais et Guinéens ravivent la flamme du panafricanisme à Conakry est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: 2027 elections: Stop the violence!
items.description: The 2027 general elections are a couple of months away, but the campaigns are already taking a dangerous turn. Barely weeks after political parties commenced electioneering, Nigeria is witnessing an alarming wave of violence, killing, intimidation, and destruction of campaign materials. This is a disturbing portent of what could happen if decisive action is not taken. The killing of Ifeanyi Nwolie, a 43-year-old supporter of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), during the violent disruption of activities surrounding the party’s governorship campaign in Enugu is particularly tragic. Suspected political thugs reportedly attacked supporters at the Akanu Ibiam International Airport and later around the party secretariat. Nwolie sustained gunshot injuries and subsequently died. His death has become another grim statistic in Nigeria’s history of political violence. Equally reprehensible was the attack on Peter Obi’s convoy in Calabar, Cross River State, by suspected hoodlums armed with machetes and sticks. Windscreens were smashed as the presidential candidate returned from a visit to the Obong of Calabar. The police subsequently announced the arrest of a suspect, Victor Edet. There was also a potentially explosive confrontation between NDC and APC supporters in the city, which security operatives managed to prevent. Meanwhile, APC campaign billboards and posters have reportedly been vandalised in Kano and other Northern cities by irate youths. APC supporters travelling to a campaign rally in Katsina were also attacked, leaving a female passenger injured. The police arrested 14 suspects, including a minor. Other reported disruptions of political activities, including Governor Alex Otti’s campaign inauguration in Abia, reinforce the need for vigilance. The Nigerian Police Force has responded by reading the riot act. Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Disu, directed Commissioners nationwide to prevent the destruction of campaign materials, intimidation and harassment. The police warned that offenders, including those sponsoring or financing such criminal activities, would be arrested and prosecuted. These are welcome assurances, but Nigerians expect action, not mere warnings. The implications are grave. Campaign violence suppresses participation, deepens political divisions and encourages retaliation. Most frightening is the possibility of a major presidential or governorship candidate being killed or seriously injured. Such an incident could trigger widespread unrest, communal reprisals and a national crisis. This must be prevented at all costs. Candidates must demonstrate leadership and patriotism. They should restrain their supporters, avoid inflammatory rhetoric, respect opponents’ rights to campaign and condemn violence without equivocation. Security agencies must investigate impartially, arrest perpetrators, prosecute their sponsors, irrespective of political affiliation and stay above board. Campaigns should be conducted through peaceful rallies, issue-based debates and robust presentations of manifestoes. Political parties must sign and honour peace accords. Violent campaigns will inevitably poison elections and their aftermath. Elections are a means to an end: choosing visionary and patriotic leaders to rescue our country. Let the people decide. Stop the violence! The post 2027 elections: Stop the violence! appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Gold gains more than 1% as softer oil prices ease inflation worries
items.description: Gold rose more than 1% on Monday ‌as softer oil prices eased inflation concerns, while investors awaited key US inflation data and fresh signals from the Federal Reserve on its policy outlook. Spot gold climbed 1.6% to $4,129.69 per ounce by ​0220 GMT, while US gold futures for December delivery rose 1.6% to $4,139.00. Bullion gained ​about 5% last week. Oil prices fell after US President Donald Trump said ⁠he was highly unlikely to order further attacks on Iran as talks to end the ​conflict continued, easing concerns about potential supply disruptions. Lower oil prices can ease inflationary pressures and ​reduce expectations that interest rates will stay higher for longer, lowering the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion. “Trump’s more conciliatory tone toward Iran is helping keep a lid on oil prices, which in ​turn eases some of the inflation pressure that had been weighing on the metal ​along with a modest pullback in the dollar,” said Tim Waterer, chief market analyst at KCM ‌Trade. The US ⁠dollar softened, making greenback-priced bullion more affordable for buyers overseas. Meanwhile, US job growth accelerated in October and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, reinforcing expectations that the labour market remains resilient and keeping the Fed on track for a December interest-rate increase. Traders currently see a ​79% chance that the ​Fed will raise ⁠rates in December, up from 71% prior to the payrolls data, according to CME’s FedWatch tool. Market participants now await the US ​Consumer Price Index data due on Tuesday and the Producer Price ​Index on ⁠Friday to further gauge the Fed’s monetary policy stance. “Any hot readings would likely firm the dollar and lift the odds of a December rate hike, which would quickly put gold ⁠back ​on the defensive,” Waterer said. Among other metals, spot silver ​climbed 2.8% to $53.31 per ounce, platinum gained 1.6% to $1,556.14 and palladium rose 2.1% to $1,044.28.

items.title: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Gilgit-Baltistan agree to settle old boundary disputes
items.description: KP Governor Faisal Karim Kundi and GB Chief Minister Amjad Hussain meet in Islamabad.—Dawn GILGIT/MANSEHRA: In a move towards resolving decades-old territorial issues, Gilgit-Baltistan Chief Minister Amjad Hussain and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi have agreed to initiate negotiations to settle boundary disputes between the two regions, including those involving Shandur Top, Babusar Top and areas surrounding the Diamer-Bhasha and Dassu dams. The agreement came during a meeting between the two leaders in Islamabad on Sunday, where they discussed matters of mutual interest, including territorial disputes, improved air connectivity to Gilgit-Baltistan and the training of relevant officials. According to a statement issued by the GB Chief Minister’s Secre­tariat, both leaders agreed that the boundary disputes would be taken up by the chief secretaries of the two regions, before being referred to their respective political leadership for deliberations. South Air offers to operate flights to northern areas The initiative aims to resolve disputes involving villages along the KP-GB boundary through mutual understanding and amicable negotiations. An official attending the meeting told Dawn that the two sides had agreed to pursue a peaceful settlement of the long-standing disputes, which have repeatedly triggered tensions and violent clashes between communities living along the disputed territories. Disputes between KP and GB persist over several strategically important areas, including Shandur Top, Babusar Top and parts of Kohistan. Shandur Top, home to the world’s highest polo ground at around 12,500 feet, is claimed by both provinces, with the matter under consideration by a provincial boundary commission. Babusar Top, linking Man­sehra with Diamer through Kaghan Valley, is another contested area whose ownership and juri­sdiction remain unresolved by the federal government. The dispute has also surfaced in land acquisition and compensation claims, prompting the Peshawar High Court to direct the NHA and KP government to clear outstanding payments to landowners whose properties were acquired in 2001 for road expansion. Another major dispute concerns the Harban tribe of Kohistan and the Thor tribe of Diamer over an eight-kilometre stretch near the Diamer-Bhasha Dam. A 2014 clash over the land claimed the lives of five people and left 15 injured. A 24-member jirga defused the decades-old dispute in 2022, paving the way for official demarcation and compensation payments to affected Kohistan settlers. However, other territorial and ownership questions, including those concerning areas near the Dassu Dam and Babusar Top, have continued to complicate relations between communities on both sides of the provincial boundary. Air connectivity Apart from territorial matters, the Islamabad meeting also focused on improving air connectivity between Gilgit and Islamabad, where passengers have long faced difficulties because of limited flight operations and frequent cancellations. At present, PIA operates a 44-seat ATR aircraft on the Islamabad-Gilgit route. The limited seating capacity, coupled with weather-related cancellations, has made air travel particularly difficult for patients, tourists and government officials who depend on the service. The operational limitations of Gilgit airport, which cannot accommodate larger aircraft, further restrict travel options. During the meeting, representatives of the private airline South Air also held discussions with the GB chief minister regarding the introduction of additional air services. According to an official source, it was agreed that aircraft would be acquired on lease against a guarantee provided by the GB government, while South Air would operate flights under a joint-venture arrangement. The proposed service is expected to introduce weather-compliant aircraft on the Isla­mabad-Gilgit route, potentially improving the reliability of air travel for residents and visitors. Published in Dawn, November 9th, 2026
